The voters accepted it in 1994, and since **1996** the insurance has been **compulsory** throughout Switzerland. Anyone who moves to Switzerland must take out insurance with a health insurer **within three months**.

In basic insurance the health insurers must **accept all people**. They may not turn anyone down because of **previous illnesses**. All insurers pay for the **same benefits**, which the federal government sets. There are differences in premium and service. That is why you can change insurer without losing benefits.

The monthly **premium** depends on the place of residence, age, the chosen **deductible** (called the “Franchise” in Switzerland) and the insurance model, but **not on income**. Anyone who earns little can get a **premium reduction** from the canton. The deductible is the amount you pay yourself per year before the insurer pays. After that you usually still bear an **excess** of 10 per cent up to an upper limit.

In the **Tiers garant** system the patient pays the bill herself and gets the money back from the insurer. In **Tiers payant** the doctor’s practice or pharmacy sends the bill directly to the insurer. **Employees** who work **at least 8 hours a week** for the same employer are insured against accidents through the employer and can exclude accident cover. **Ordinary dental treatment** such as fillings is usually not paid for by basic insurance.

Anyone who wants more, for example a single room in hospital, can take out **supplementary insurance**. It is governed by the **Insurance Contract Act (VVG)**. Here insurers may ask **health questions** and turn down applications.

gewusst: Before 1996 health insurance was not compulsory everywhere in Switzerland, but in some cantons it was.
You can change your health insurer every year at the start of the new year.

teile.einleitung: Narcolepsy is a rare disease of the brain in which the control of sleeping and waking is disturbed. People affected are very sleepy during the day and can suddenly fall asleep.
wichtigste: Narcolepsy is a chronic disorder of the control of sleep and waking.
Typical is strong sleepiness during the day.
In type 1 cataplexy occurs, in type 2 it does not.
In type 1 the messenger substance orexin, also called hypocretin, is missing.
REM sleep often begins soon after falling asleep.
Sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations are common.
In the sleep laboratory the multiple sleep latency test helps with the diagnosis.

abschnitte.text: Normally our brain switches reliably between being awake and being asleep. In **narcolepsy** this control is disturbed. People affected are constantly very tired during the day and can even fall asleep in the middle of an activity. In **narcolepsy type 1** certain nerve cells in the **hypothalamus** are lost. They make the messenger substance **orexin**, also called **hypocretin**, which keeps the waking state stable.

A special sign is **cataplexy**. In it the muscles suddenly lose their tension. It is triggered by strong **feelings**, for example when laughing or at a surprise. Sometimes only the head droops, and sometimes the knees buckle. The people affected stay **conscious** while this happens. In **narcolepsy type 2** there is sleepiness during the day, but no cataplexy.

abschnitte.titel: Dream sleep in the wrong place
abschnitte.text: Normally the first **REM sleep**, the phase with vivid dreams, begins only after about 90 minutes. In narcolepsy it often comes within 15 minutes. Parts of dream sleep also break into the waking state. This is how **hypnagogic hallucinations** arise, vivid, dream-like impressions when falling asleep. In **sleep paralysis** you cannot move a single muscle for a short time on waking up, although you are awake. It also occurs in healthy people.

In the **sleep laboratory** sleep and brain waves are measured. In the **multiple sleep latency test** the person may lie down several times spread over the day. Short times to fall asleep and early REM phases point to narcolepsy. After vaccination with the vaccine **Pandemrix** against **swine flu in 2009**, more cases occurred, especially in Scandinavia. A reaction of the immune system against the body’s own cells in people with a certain predisposition is suspected.

gewusst: To this day narcolepsy cannot be cured, but it can be treated well with medicines and planned naps.
Dogs too can get narcolepsy, and this helped researchers to find the cause.

teile.einleitung: Earache is very common in children. Usually an inflammation in the ear is behind it, often after a cold. It hurts, but in many cases it heals again after a few days.
wichtigste: A common cause in children is middle ear infection.
Earache often comes after a cold.
The Eustachian tube joins the middle ear to the throat.
With strong pain or fever you go to the doctor.
You must never put pointed objects into the ear.
A hat protects the ears from cold wind.

abschnitte.text: Behind the eardrum lies the **middle ear**, a small space with air. It is joined to the **throat** by the **Eustachian tube**, a narrow passage. In a **cold** this passage swells, and germs can get into the middle ear. Then a **middle ear infection** arises. In children the Eustachian tube is shorter, which is why it affects them especially often.

After **bathing** or swimming, **water** sometimes stays **in the ear canal**. This can irritate the skin and cause an inflammation of the ear canal. **Cold wind** can also make the ears hurt, which is why a **hat** helps. When flying or in the mountains the ears often feel pressure when the air pressure changes quickly. Swallowing or yawning then helps.

If the ear **hurts a lot**, **fever** is added or fluid runs out of the ear, you should go to the **doctor**. She looks into the ear with an **otoscope**. This is a small light with a funnel. With it she sees whether the eardrum is red. Often painkillers and nose drops help, and sometimes an **antibiotic** is needed.

You must **never put pointed objects** into the ear, not even cotton buds deep into the ear canal. They can injure the sensitive **eardrum**. A lot of rest, drinking enough and warmth, on the other hand, often do good.

gewusst: The Eustachian tube is named after the Italian doctor Bartolomeo Eustachi.
Many children have a middle ear infection at least once before school age.

teile.einleitung: The maximum heart rate is the highest number of heartbeats per minute that a person can reach at greatest effort. In sport it helps to steer training correctly. You can estimate it roughly or measure it exactly.
wichtigste: A simple rule of thumb is: 220 minus your age.
For a 14-year-old this gives 206 beats per minute.
The maximum heart rate falls with age.
It is determined more precisely with an exercise test.
Easy basic training is at about 60 to 70 per cent.
You can feel the pulse well at the wrist.
A heart rate watch with a sensor measures the pulse continuously.

abschnitte.text: With every beat the **heart** pumps blood into the arteries. You can feel this pressure wave as the **pulse**. You can feel it well at the **wrist** on the thumb side or at the side of the neck. You count the beats for 15 seconds, for example, and multiply by 4. This gives the beats per minute. When you exert yourself, the heart beats faster, until it reaches the **maximum heart rate**.

A well-known rule of thumb is: **220 minus your age**. For a 14-year-old this gives 220 minus 14, that is **206** beats per minute. The formula also shows that the maximum heart rate **falls with age**. But it is only a rough guide. In many people the real value is clearly higher or lower.

The maximum heart rate is determined more precisely with an **exercise test**. In this you increase the effort step by step, for example on a treadmill or a bike, until you cannot go on. Such a test should only be done when healthy and best of all under guidance. In sport, a **heart rate watch with a sensor** measures the pulse continuously, either at the wrist or with a chest strap.

With the maximum heart rate you can work out **training zones**. Easy **basic training** is at about **60 to 70 per cent** of the maximum heart rate. In this you can still talk well. An example: if someone has a maximum heart rate of 200, 70 per cent of that is **140** beats per minute. Harder training is higher but is held only briefly.

gewusst: A trained heart often beats more slowly at rest than an untrained one.
The maximum heart rate can hardly be raised by training, but the resting heart rate can fall.

teile.einleitung: Malaria is a dangerous infectious disease that occurs in warm countries. It is caused by tiny parasites and passed on by mosquitoes. Every year very many people around the world fall ill with it.
wichtigste: Malaria is passed on by the Anopheles mosquito.
Only the females bite and pass on the disease.
Recurring attacks of fever are typical.
The germs multiply in the red blood cells.
Most cases occur in Africa south of the Sahara.
A mosquito net protects especially well at night.
World Malaria Day is on 25 April.

abschnitte.text: The name **malaria** comes from the Italian expression **“mala aria”**, which means **“bad air”**. In the past people believed that the disease was caused by the damp air in marshes. Today we know that tiny single-celled **parasites** cause the disease. They are called **plasmodia**. Many mosquitoes live in marshy areas, though, and so the old idea had a grain of truth.

Malaria is passed on by the **Anopheles mosquito**. **Only the females** bite, because they need blood to make eggs. When a mosquito bites a sick person, it takes in germs. At the next bite it can pass them on to another person. The mosquitoes bite mainly at dusk and at night.

The germs first get into the **liver**. After that they enter the **red blood cells** and multiply there. When the blood cells burst, new germs are set free. This leads to **recurring attacks of fever** with shivering and sweating. Without treatment malaria can become life-threatening, especially for small children.

Malaria occurs in tropical and subtropical regions. The **most cases** occur in **Africa south of the Sahara**. The disease does not occur in Switzerland. But travellers can catch it in malaria regions. That is why they get advice before the journey, for example at a travel medicine clinic. Every year on **25 April** it is **World Malaria Day**.

A simple and effective protection is a **mosquito net** over the bed, often treated with an insect repellent. Long clothes and mosquito repellent on the skin also help. An old drug against malaria is **quinine**. It comes from the bark of the **cinchona tree** from South America. Today there are other medicines and now also vaccines for children in malaria regions.

gewusst: Quinine gives tonic water its bitter taste.
The Chinese scientist Tu Youyou received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2015 for discovering the malaria drug artemisinin.
Because of diseases like malaria, mosquitoes are regarded as the most dangerous animals in the world for humans.

teile.einleitung: Nicotine is a substance from the tobacco plant. It is the main reason why smoking makes people addicted so quickly. Nicotine is found in cigarettes, e-cigarettes and snus.
wichtigste: Nicotine comes from the tobacco plant.
Of all the substances in tobacco it causes the strongest addiction.
When smoking, nicotine reaches the brain within a few seconds.
Nicotine narrows the blood vessels.
The name goes back to the Frenchman Jean Nicot.
Passive smoking also harms health.

abschnitte.text: The **tobacco plant** comes from America and makes nicotine to protect itself from insects. That is why nicotine was once also used as an **insecticide**. The substance is named after **Jean Nicot**, a French envoy in the 16th century. He brought tobacco to the French court.

When smoking, nicotine gets into the blood through the lungs and reaches the brain **within a few seconds**. There it releases messenger substances that briefly produce a pleasant feeling. The body gets used to it quickly, and an **addiction** arises. Nicotine **narrows the blood vessels** and makes the heart beat faster.

In tobacco smoke there are many other poisons besides nicotine. **Carbon monoxide** is a gas that binds to the red blood cells and hinders the transport of oxygen. Tar and other substances can cause cancer. Anyone who breathes in other people’s smoke is doing **passive smoking**. That is why smoking is banned in many enclosed spaces in Switzerland.

In an **e-cigarette** a liquid, the **e-liquid**, is heated and breathed in as vapour. Many e-liquids contain nicotine and also cause addiction. **Snus** is damp tobacco in small pouches that you put under the **upper lip**. In this way too nicotine gets into the blood. Since 2024 tobacco products and e-cigarettes may not be sold to people under 18 anywhere in Switzerland.

gewusst: The tobacco plant belongs to the same family as the potato and the tomato, the nightshades.
The scientific name of the genus of the tobacco plant is Nicotiana, also after Jean Nicot.

teile.einleitung: Through the nostrils air flows into our nose. Many animals have nostrils too, some in quite astonishing places.
wichtigste: Through the nostrils air gets into the nasal cavity.
You do not put small objects into the nostrils.
In horses and cattle the nostrils are called “Nüstern” in German.
The elephant has its nostrils at the front of the trunk.
The kiwi has them at the tip of its beak.
Hippos can close their nostrils when diving.
In the crocodile they sit on top of the tip of the snout.

abschnitte.text: Humans have two **nostrils**. Through them air flows into the **nasal cavity**, the space behind the nostrils. From there it goes on into the throat. The two nostrils are separated by the **nasal septum**. Small objects such as beads or peas never belong in a nostril. They can get stuck, and then a doctor often has to help.

In **horses** and cattle the nostrils are called **“Nüstern”** in German. Horses can open them wide when they need a lot of air. The nose of a **dog** is usually **moist** around the nostrils. On the moist skin scent particles stick well. This lets the dog notice smells even better.

The trunk of the **elephant** is a very long nose that has grown together with the upper lip. Right at the front lie the two nostrils. With the trunk the elephant can smell, suck up water and grasp things. The **kiwi** from **New Zealand** is a bird that has its nostrils at the **tip of its long beak**. This lets it smell worms in the ground.

Animals that live a lot in water have special noses. The **hippo** can **close** its nostrils when it dives, so that no water runs in. In the **crocodile** the nostrils lie **on top of the tip of the snout**. This lets it breathe while it lies almost completely under water, lying in wait for prey. Whales, too, have their nasal opening on top of the head: the **blowhole**.

gewusst: The kiwi is one of the few birds with a really good sense of smell.
Dolphins and whales do not breathe through the mouth, but only through the blowhole.

teile.einleitung: The genetic material of every cell is stored in the DNA. Sometimes this DNA changes, and this is called a **mutation**. Many mutations are harmless, some can cause diseases, and some are the reason for the variety of living things.
wichtigste: A mutation is a lasting change in the genetic material.
In a substitution one base is swapped for another.
The deletion of a base usually shifts the reading frame.
A silent mutation does not change the amino acids.
A nonsense mutation produces a premature stop codon.
UV radiation causes thymine dimers.
Substances or rays that cause mutations are called mutagens.

abschnitte.text: DNA is read in groups of three, the **codons**. Each codon stands for an amino acid, from which proteins are built. In a **substitution** a single base is swapped for another, and the length of the DNA stays the same. This is a form of **point mutation**. If a single base is missing, this is called a **deletion**. Then all the following groups of three shift, the **reading frame** is shifted, and usually a completely changed protein results.

Not every point mutation has consequences. Because several codons can stand for the same amino acid, the protein sometimes stays the same. This is a **silent mutation**. In a **missense mutation** a different amino acid is built in. The consequences range from harmless to severe, and a well-known example is sickle cell anaemia. In a **nonsense mutation** a **premature stop codon** arises. The protein becomes too short and usually does not work.

Some mutations arise by chance when the cell copies its DNA. Others are triggered by **mutagens**. These are substances or rays that raise the mutation rate, for example ionising radiation, UV light and certain chemicals in tobacco smoke. **UV light** links two neighbouring thymines together to form **thymine dimers**. If they are not repaired, mutations and skin cancer can arise. That is why sun protection is so important in Switzerland, especially in the mountains.

Mutations can also affect whole chromosomes. In a **genome mutation** the number of chromosomes is changed. One example is **trisomy 21**: chromosome 21 is present three times instead of twice. People with trisomy 21 have Down’s syndrome. Cells also have **repair systems** of their own that put right many kinds of damage to the DNA.

gewusst: The term mutation was coined around 1901 by the Dutch botanist Hugo de Vries.
Without mutations there would be no evolution, because they provide the differences between living things.

teile.einleitung: Phones, games and social media are fun and part of everyday life. But some people can hardly stop using them, even when it harms them. This is then called media addiction.
wichtigste: The WHO has included gaming disorder in the ICD-11.
One warning sign is when you neglect friends and school.
FOMO means the fear of missing out.
Bright screen light in the evening slows the sleep hormone melatonin.
Likes work through the messenger substance dopamine.
The Swiss JAMES study investigates how young people use media.
Charging your phone outside the bedroom helps you to sleep.

abschnitte.titel: When does it become an addiction?
abschnitte.text: Not every long time on the phone is an addiction. We speak of **media addiction** when someone loses control and carries on despite the disadvantages. **Warning signs** are, for example, when you **neglect friends and school**, give up hobbies or get irritable when you cannot be online. The World Health Organization **WHO** has included **gaming disorder** as a disease in its list **ICD-11**.

When we get a **like** or win something in a game, the brain releases the messenger substance **dopamine**. It belongs to the **reward system** and gives a good feeling. That is why we want more of it. Some apps are designed for exactly this. With **endless scrolling** the content never ends, and so you keep swiping on.

New terms have arisen around the phone. **FOMO** stands for “fear of missing out”, that is, the **fear of missing something**. It makes many people check constantly. **Phubbing** is when someone ignores the person in front of them and looks at their phone instead. The word is made up of “phone” and “snubbing”, which means ignoring someone rudely.

Screens give off bright, bluish light. In the evening it slows the making of the sleep hormone **melatonin**. You get tired later and sleep worse. In addition there are messages that wake you in the night. A simple help is to **charge your phone outside the bedroom** and to use no more screens for an hour before sleep.

The **JAMES study** has regularly investigated since 2010 how young people in Switzerland use media. It is carried out by ZHAW and Swisscom. Anyone who notices that their use of media is becoming a problem can talk to parents, teachers or school social work. Help is also available around the clock from the advice service of **Pro Juventute** on the number **147**.

gewusst: JAMES stands for “Jugend, Aktivitäten, Medien, Erhebung Schweiz”, which means Youth, Activities, Media, Survey Switzerland.
Many phones have a function that shows how long you have spent on the screen in a day.

teile.einleitung: Nervous tissue forms the brain, spinal cord and nerves. It consists of nerve cells, which conduct signals, and glial cells, which support and protect them.
wichtigste: Nervous tissue consists of nerve cells and glial cells.
Nerve cells conduct and process signals.
Schwann cells make the insulating myelin layer in the peripheral nervous system.
At the nodes of Ranvier the excitation jumps from place to place.
Microglial cells are the defence cells of the brain.
Astrocytes are an important part of the blood-brain barrier.
At the synapse the signal is passed on with messenger substances.

abschnitte.text: Nervous tissue consists of two cell types. The **nerve cells**, also called **neurons**, conduct and process signals. The **glial cells** support, feed and insulate the nerve cells. A nerve cell has fine extensions, the **dendrites**, which take in signals. A long extension, the **axon**, passes the signal on.

At the **axon hillock**, where the axon starts from the cell body, all incoming signals are added up. If a threshold is exceeded, an **action potential** arises, which runs along the axon. At the end the nerve cell passes the signal on at a **synapse**. There **neurotransmitters** are released into a narrow gap. They bind to receptors of the next cell and trigger a reaction there.

Many axons are wrapped in an insulating layer of **myelin**. In the peripheral nervous system it is made by the **Schwann cells**, which wind several times around an axon. In the brain and spinal cord **oligodendrocytes** take on this job. Between two sections of myelin lie free places, the **nodes of Ranvier**. Only there does the action potential arise, and the excitation jumps from node to node. This **saltatory conduction** is much faster than continuous conduction.

**Microglial cells** are the resident **defence cells** of the brain. They remove germs, dead cells and waste. **Astrocytes** are star-shaped glial cells. With their little feet they enclose the fine blood vessels in the brain. Together with the tightly joined cells of the vessels they form the **blood-brain barrier**. It controls which substances get from the blood into the brain.

gewusst: The word glia comes from the Greek word for glue, because people used to think it only held the nerve cells together.
In the brain there are about as many glial cells as nerve cells.

teile.einleitung: When we lift an arm, an order has to pass from the nerve to the muscle. This happens at the **motor end plate**, a special point of contact between a nerve cell and a muscle fibre.
wichtigste: The motor end plate is the synapse between a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fibre.
The messenger substance is acetylcholine.
An inflow of calcium into the nerve ending triggers its release.
In the muscle membrane sit nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
Each end plate potential normally triggers an action potential.
Myasthenia gravis, curare and botulinum toxin disturb the transmission.

abschnitte.titel: From the nerve to the muscle
abschnitte.text: A **motor neuron** is a nerve cell that controls muscles. Its end lies close to a skeletal muscle fibre. This point of contact is called the **motor end plate** or neuromuscular synapse. Here the electrical signal of the nerve is turned into a chemical signal. A motor neuron and all the muscle fibres that it controls together form a **motor unit**. In the eye muscles there are only a few fibres, and in large leg muscles often hundreds to over a thousand.

When an action potential arrives at the nerve ending, voltage-gated **calcium channels** open. The calcium flowing in makes small sacs release their contents, the messenger substance **acetylcholine**. It binds to **nicotinic acetylcholine receptors** in the muscle membrane. These receptors are ion channels that open directly. Mainly **sodium** flows in, a little potassium flows out, and the membrane is depolarised. An enzyme then quickly breaks the acetylcholine down again.

The **end plate potential** that arises in this way is very large. It safely exceeds the threshold and normally triggers an **action potential** in the muscle fibre every time. This is called a high **safety factor**. This is important so that our movements work reliably. Unlike in the brain, nothing is calculated here, and the signal is simply passed on.

In the disease **myasthenia gravis**, the immune system makes antibodies against the acetylcholine receptors. Muscle weakness that gets worse with exertion is typical. The arrow poison **curare** occupies the receptors without opening them, and the muscles are paralysed limp. **Botulinum toxin**, on the other hand, prevents the release of acetylcholine. It splits proteins that the sacs need in order to fuse with the membrane.

gewusst: Curare was used by peoples in South America for hunting with arrows.
Active substances derived from curare are used today in operations to relax muscles.

teile.einleitung: **Mumps** is a contagious viral disease. Typical are fat cheeks, because the salivary glands swell up. Thanks to vaccination, mumps is much rarer today than it used to be.
wichtigste: Mumps is a contagious viral disease.
It is caused by the mumps virus.
The parotid glands swell, and the face looks as if it had hamster cheeks.
You catch it through droplets of saliva.
Often there is also fever and a headache.
In Germany mumps is also called “Ziegenpeter”.
Since the vaccination became available, mumps has been much rarer in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: In mumps the **parotid glands** swell. They lie in front of and below the ears and make saliva. When they get fat, the face looks like that of a hamster with full cheeks. Often one side swells first and then the other. The swelling is painful, and **chewing** can hurt too. Many children also have a **fever** and a headache and feel weak.

Mumps is caused by the **mumps virus** and passes from person to person. The virus is in the **saliva**. It can be passed on by coughing, sneezing, a kiss on the cheek or drinking from the same glass. Until the first signs appear, usually two to three weeks go by. Some people notice almost nothing of an infection.

There is no special medicine against the virus itself. Anyone who has mumps should **stay at home and rest**. That way you recover better and do not infect anyone. Soft foods are more pleasant, because chewing hurts. For fever and pain the doctor can recommend something. Usually the illness is over after about one to two weeks.

In the past almost every child got mumps, and it was a typical **childhood disease**. Today there is a vaccination, which is usually given together against measles, mumps and rubella. In Switzerland it is recommended for children, in two doses. Since then **far fewer** children get mumps. In Germany the disease is also called **“Ziegenpeter”**, a very old word.

gewusst: Anyone who has had mumps once is usually protected from it for life.
The parotid gland is the largest salivary gland of the human body.

teile.einleitung: **Multiple sclerosis**, MS for short, is a disease of the central nervous system. The body’s own immune system attacks the protective layer around the nerve fibres. The disease runs a different course in every person.
wichtigste: MS is a chronic inflammatory autoimmune disease.
The brain, spinal cord and optic nerves are affected.
The immune system attacks the myelin sheaths of the nerve fibres.
Women are affected about 2 to 3 times as often as men.
The disease usually begins between the ages of 20 and 40.
At the start it usually comes in relapses.
MS lesions can best be shown with an MRI scan.

abschnitte.text: Many nerve fibres are wrapped in a fatty layer, the **myelin sheaths**. They work like insulation and make sure that signals are passed on quickly. In **multiple sclerosis** the body’s own immune system attacks this layer. **Areas of inflammation** appear and later scars, hence the name: sclerosis means hardening, and multiple means many. The **central nervous system** is affected, that is, the brain, spinal cord and optic nerves. The peripheral nerves are usually spared.

MS usually begins in young adulthood, **between the ages of 20 and 40**. It is a common cause of neurological disability in young adults. Like many autoimmune diseases, it affects **women** clearly more often, about 2 to 3 times as often as men. The reasons for this are not yet fully understood. MS is not contagious.

In most people affected, MS at first runs a **relapsing-remitting** course. This means that relapses with new complaints occur, which then go away completely or in part. Later it can turn into a progressive course. A common first sign is an **inflammation of the optic nerve** with blurred vision and pain when moving the eyes. Numbness, tiredness and unsteadiness when walking also occur.

Many people affected notice that their complaints get temporarily worse in **heat**, for example in a hot bath. This is called the **Uhthoff phenomenon**. Heat makes conduction in the damaged nerve fibres worse, and when you cool down it improves again. For the diagnosis, **magnetic resonance imaging** (MRI) is central, because the lesions in the white matter can be seen well in it. MS cannot yet be cured, but medicines can make relapses clearly less frequent.

gewusst: Switzerland is one of the countries where MS is comparatively common.
The name multiple sclerosis describes the many hardened scars in the nervous system.

teile.einleitung: Nails are the hard plates at the ends of our fingers and toes. They protect the sensitive fingertips and help us to grip small things. Nails consist of horn, the same material as hair.
wichtigste: Fingernails protect the sensitive fingertips.
Nails consist of keratin, a firm horn protein.
They grow from the nail root under the skin.
Fingernails grow about 3 millimetres a month, and toenails more slowly.
Nails help us to grip small things and to scratch.
Cutting nails does not hurt, because they have no nerves.
Changed nails can give hints of diseases.

abschnitte.text: The **nail** is a hard, slightly curved plate on the upper side of the tips of the fingers and toes. It consists of **keratin**, a firm protein that hair and the top layer of skin are also made of. The nail itself is dead, which is why cutting it does not hurt. Humans and other apes have nails, and many other animals have claws or hooves of similar material instead.

The visible part is called the **nail plate**. Beneath it lies the nail bed, which has a good blood supply and makes the nail shimmer pink. At the bottom of the nail you often see a white half moon, the lunula. Behind it, under the skin, lies the **nail root**, where new nail cells are constantly made. A thin little skin, the cuticle, protects the root from dirt and germs.

Nails protect the sensitive fingertips from injuries. They form a firm support so that we can feel and grip things better with the finger pads. With our nails we pick up small objects, open fasteners, scratch or peel an orange. Without nails the fingertips would be much less skilful.

Fingernails grow about 3 millimetres a month, and toenails only about one millimetre. A whole fingernail is completely renewed in about half a year. In summer and in children nails grow a little faster. On the hand you write with they often grow a little faster.

You should cut nails regularly, fingernails rather round and toenails straight, so that they do not grow in. An **ingrown toenail** can become inflamed and hurt a lot. Nail fungus makes nails thick, yellowish and brittle. White spots in the nail usually come from small knocks and are harmless.

begriffe.erklaerung: A firm protein that nails and hair are made of.
The skin under the nail on which it rests.
The place under the skin where the nail grows.
The pale half moon at the lower end of the nail.

gewusst: Nails do not keep growing after death, it only looks that way because the skin dries out and pulls back.
The nails on the middle finger usually grow fastest, and on the little finger slowest.
Doctors sometimes look at the nails during examinations, because they can give hints of diseases.

teile.einleitung: The stomach is a muscular bag in the upper belly where food lands after we have swallowed it. There the food is mixed with gastric juice and broken down further. The stomach is an important station on the long journey of digestion.
wichtigste: After swallowing, food passes through the gullet into the stomach.
In the stomach the food is mixed with gastric juice and broken down.
Gastric juice contains hydrochloric acid, which makes bacteria harmless.
The enzyme pepsin begins the digestion of protein in the stomach.
A layer of mucus protects the stomach wall from its own acid.
In adults the stomach holds about 1.5 litres.
Stomach rumbling often happens when the stomach is empty and contracts.

abschnitte.text: The **stomach** lies in the upper left of the belly, directly below the diaphragm. It has the shape of a curved sack or a bean. At the top the gullet opens into the stomach, and at the bottom it passes into the small intestine. When empty it is quite small, and after a big meal it can stretch a lot.

The stomach wall consists of strong muscles that tighten in waves. This kneads the food pulp, mixes it and breaks it down further. Depending on the meal, food stays in the stomach for about two to four hours, and fatty food for longer. Then the **pylorus**, a ring-shaped muscle at the exit of the stomach, lets the pulp out into the small intestine in portions.

The lining of the stomach makes about two to three litres of **gastric juice** a day. It contains **hydrochloric acid**, which is so strong that it kills most of the bacteria in food. The enzyme pepsin begins to break down protein from meat, cheese or eggs. So that the stomach does not digest itself, a thick layer of mucus protects it.

Even when the stomach is empty, it contracts regularly to push remains along. In doing so, air and liquid are pushed around, which makes gurgling sounds. Because there is no food to muffle the noises, you can hear **stomach rumbling** especially well when the stomach is empty. So it is quite normal and usually a sign of hunger.

Eating too much, too fatty food or too fast can cause tummy ache or heartburn. In **heartburn**, stomach acid rises into the gullet and burns there. In a stomach bug you often have to be sick, and the muscles then press the contents of the stomach upwards. The bacterium Helicobacter pylori can cause stomach ulcers.

Eating slowly and chewing well takes the strain off the stomach, because it has no teeth. Regular meals and enough water are good for it. After eating, a short walk is better than wild romping about. The feeling of being full comes only about 20 minutes after you start eating, so if you wolf your food you can easily eat too much.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tube of muscle that brings food from the mouth to the stomach.
An acid liquid in the stomach that digests food and kills germs.
A ring muscle at the exit of the stomach that lets the food pulp into the intestine.
A protein that breaks food down into smaller building blocks.

gewusst: The lining of the stomach renews itself every few days, so that the acid does not destroy it.
Gastric juice has a pH value of about 1 to 2 and is therefore even more acid than lemon juice.
For discovering that bacteria cause stomach ulcers, Barry Marshall and Robin Warren received the Nobel Prize in 2005.

teile.einleitung: A mole is a small, usually brown spot on the skin. Almost everyone has some, and most of the time they are completely harmless.
wichtigste: A mole is a place with especially many colour cells in the skin.
In German it is also called “Leberfleck” (liver spot), but it has nothing to do with the liver.
Most moles are light to dark brown.
Many moles only appear in childhood and youth.
Sun can contribute to new moles appearing.
If a mole changes a lot, you show it to a skin doctor.

abschnitte.text: In our skin there are **colour cells** that make a brown pigment. This pigment is called **melanin**. In some places many of these cells gather in a small space. There you then see a brown spot: a mole. Because the colour sits inside the skin, you cannot wash a mole off.

In German a mole is called “Muttermal” (literally “mother mark”) and also **“Leberfleck”** (literally “liver spot”). The second name comes from the colour, which is a little like liver. But the spot has nothing to do with the organ, the liver. Experts speak of a **naevus**. Some moles are flat, and others bulge a little out of the skin.

Some people have a mole at birth. But most appear only in **childhood and youth**. How many someone gets also depends on the family. The **sun** plays a part as well: anyone who is often in the sun for a long time without protection usually gets more moles. That is why sun cream, a hat and shade are important.

Small, round moles that do not change are almost always harmless. You should take it seriously if a mole **grows quickly**, changes its shape or colour, itches or bleeds. Rarely, a form of **skin cancer** can arise from it. Then you show the mole to a **skin doctor**. She can examine it closely with a special magnifying glass and remove it if necessary.

gewusst: Many adults have dozens of moles on their body.
Skin doctors are called dermatologists in technical language.

teile.einleitung: The upper arm bone is the only bone in the upper arm. It reaches from the shoulder to the elbow. Experts call it the humerus.
wichtigste: The upper arm has only one bone, the upper arm bone.
Its Latin name is humerus.
It takes part in the shoulder joint and the elbow joint.
The round upper end is called the head of the humerus.
The radial nerve runs in a spiral around its shaft.
In older people it often breaks near the shoulder.

abschnitte.text: The **upper arm bone** is a long **tubular bone** and belongs to the **upper limb**, that is, the arm. At the top it carries the round **head of the humerus**. Beside it lie two bony lumps, the **greater** and the **lesser tubercle**. Between them lies the long shaft. At the bottom the bone becomes wider and forms the joint surfaces for the elbow.

The head of the humerus sits in a shallow socket of the shoulder blade. This creates the **shoulder joint**, the most mobile joint of the body. At the bottom the upper arm bone forms the **elbow joint** with the **ulna** and **radius**. With it we can bend and straighten the arm.

Shoulder muscles attach to the tubercles, holding and turning the joint. The large **deltoid muscle** attaches at the side of the shaft and lifts the arm sideways. In a groove around the shaft the **radial nerve** runs in a spiral. It controls the muscles that straighten the hand and fingers. In a break of the shaft it can be injured.

If older people fall onto an outstretched arm, the upper arm bone often breaks at the **upper end near the shoulder**. One reason is that bones become thinner with age. Many such breaks heal with a sling and physiotherapy, and some have to be operated on.

gewusst: The so-called “funny bone” at the elbow is actually a nerve, the ulnar nerve, which runs there just under the skin past the upper arm bone.
In German it is called “Musikantenknochen”, literally “musician’s bone”, and in English “funny bone”, a pun on “humerus”.

teile.einleitung: The **middle finger** stands exactly in the middle of the hand. In almost all people it is the longest finger and helps us with writing, playing music and gripping.
wichtigste: The middle finger is the longest finger in most people.
It lies between the index finger and the ring finger.
In piano playing it has the number 3.
When taking an oath in Switzerland you raise the thumb, index finger and middle finger.
From writing, a hard spot often forms on the middle finger.
To snap your fingers you need your thumb and middle finger.

abschnitte.text: Each hand has five fingers: thumb, index finger, middle finger, ring finger and little finger. The **middle finger** stands in the middle. On one side lies the **index finger**, on the other the **ring finger**. In almost all people it is the **longest finger**. Like the index, ring and little fingers, it consists of three finger bones, while the thumb has only two.

In **piano playing** each finger gets a number. You count from the thumb: thumb 1, index finger 2, **middle finger 3**, ring finger 4 and little finger 5. In piano music these numbers are often written above the notes. This way you know which finger to press a key with. This is the same for the left and the right hand.

In Switzerland, when taking an **oath**, you raise three fingers: **thumb, index finger and middle finger**. The ring finger and little finger stay bent. This is how, for example, newly elected members of parliaments swear when they take the oath. The **Rütli Oath** is also often shown with this oath hand. The three fingers are traditionally taken as a sign of the Trinity.

When writing, the pen usually rests on the **middle finger**. The pressure makes a small hard spot, a callus, appear there on many schoolchildren. The middle finger also helps with **snapping**: you press it firmly against the thumb, then it slips off and strikes the heel of the hand. This makes the typical sound.

gewusst: The callus from writing protects the skin, and it gets smaller if you write less by hand.
The sound when snapping arises mainly when the middle finger strikes the heel of the hand.

teile.einleitung: A skeletal muscle consists of many long cells, the **muscle fibres**. They are densely packed with fine protein threads that can slide into one another. This is how the muscle contracts.
wichtigste: A muscle fibre is a single skeletal muscle cell.
It has many cell nuclei.
Muscle fibres are filled with myofibrils.
The smallest working unit of a myofibril is the sarcomere.
Actin and myosin slide past each other during contraction.
ATP supplies the energy for this.
A whole muscle is wrapped in a fascia.

abschnitte.text: In skeletal muscle, a single long muscle cell is called a **muscle fibre**. It can grow to several centimetres long. A muscle fibre arises from many fused precursor cells and therefore has **many cell nuclei**. Several fibres are gathered into bundles, and many bundles form a muscle. A whole muscle is surrounded by a sheath of tough connective tissue, the **fascia**. It holds everything together and lets neighbouring muscles glide past each other.

Each muscle fibre is filled along its length with many thin threads, the **myofibrils**. A myofibril consists of many sections lying one behind the other, the **sarcomeres**. The sarcomere is the smallest working unit of the muscle. In contraction each sarcomere becomes a little shorter. Because thousands lie one behind the other, the whole muscle becomes noticeably shorter.

In the sarcomeres lie two proteins: thin threads of **actin** and thicker ones of **myosin**. The myosin heads grab the actin threads and pull on them. In this way the threads slide into one another, and the muscle shortens. The energy for this is supplied by **ATP** (adenosine triphosphate), the direct energy carrier of the cell. Without ATP, actin and myosin cannot move.

Not all muscle fibres are the same. **Slow red fibres** (type I) have many mitochondria and a lot of red muscle pigment. They tire slowly and are suited to endurance. Fast fibres, on the other hand, quickly supply a lot of force but soon tire. With regular strength training the fibres mainly become **thicker**, which is called hypertrophy.

gewusst: The name sarcomere comes from Greek and means roughly “piece of flesh”.
Under the microscope skeletal muscle fibres look striped, because actin and myosin are arranged regularly.

teile.einleitung: The nervous system is the control and message network of your body. It notices stimuli, processes them and sends orders to muscles and organs. Billions of nerve cells work together in a flash.
wichtigste: The nervous system consists of billions of nerve cells, the neurons.
The central nervous system consists of the brain and spinal cord.
The nerves in the rest of the body form the peripheral nervous system.
At a synapse one nerve cell passes its signal on to the next cell.
Reflexes run through the spinal cord and are therefore especially fast.
The sympathetic system gets the body ready for fight or flight under stress.
The parasympathetic system provides rest, recovery and digestion.

abschnitte.text: The **central nervous system** consists of the brain and spinal cord. It is the control centre that evaluates information and makes decisions. The **peripheral nervous system** includes all the nerves that run from there into the arms, legs, skin and organs. Together the nerve pathways of one person are many thousands of kilometres long.

The building blocks of the nervous system are nerve cells, also called **neurons**. They pass on electrical signals, sometimes at over 100 metres per second. At the **synapse** the signal jumps to the next cell with the help of messenger substances. The brain alone has about 86 billion neurons.

If you touch a hot hob, you pull your hand away before you even feel pain. This is a **reflex** that runs directly through the spinal cord. The brain is informed only afterwards. This detour saves valuable time and protects you from injuries.

The **autonomic nervous system** works without your will and controls heartbeat, breathing and digestion. Its part the **sympathetic system** gets the body ready for fight or flight under stress: pulse and blood pressure rise. The **parasympathetic system** is its opposite number and provides rest and digestion. The two work like an accelerator and a brake.

The brain and spinal cord are well protected by bones, membranes and fluid. Even so, accidents when cycling or skiing can cause serious damage. A helmet therefore protects the head very effectively. Enough sleep helps the nervous system to recover and to store what has been learned.

begriffe.erklaerung: The technical word for a nerve cell.
A point of contact where a nerve cell passes a signal on to the next cell.
An automatic, lightning-fast reaction without thinking.
The part of the nervous system that activates the body under stress.
The part of the nervous system that provides rest and recovery.

gewusst: A signal from the toe to the brain takes only a fraction of a second.
The intestine also has a nerve network of its own with millions of nerve cells, which is sometimes called the gut brain.
The brain uses about a fifth of the body’s energy, although it makes up only about 2 per cent of body weight.

teile.einleitung: A nosebleed often looks bad, but in children it is usually harmless. With a few simple steps it soon stops again.
wichtigste: Nosebleeds are common in children and usually harmless.
At the front of the nose lie many fine blood vessels.
You hold the head tilted slightly forwards.
You press the soft wings of the nose together for about 10 minutes.
A cool cloth on the neck can help.
Picking the nose and dry air from heating can trigger nosebleeds.
If it does not stop for a long time, you need a doctor.

abschnitte.text: At the front of the nose, on the nasal septum, many **fine blood vessels** lie just under the lining. They are injured easily. Common triggers are heavy **nose picking**, firm nose blowing or a knock against the nose. Very **dry air from heating** in winter also makes the lining brittle, so that it bleeds more easily.

In a nosebleed you sit down and bend the head **slightly forwards**. That way the blood runs out of the nose and not into the throat. Do **not tip the head back**: otherwise the blood flows into the throat and is swallowed. This can make you feel sick. In addition you then cannot see how strongly it is still bleeding.

abschnitte.titel: Pressing the wings of the nose together
abschnitte.text: You press the **soft wings of the nose** together gently, not the hard bone at the top. This closes off the small blood vessels. You hold for about **10 minutes** without a break, so that the wound can close. A **cool cloth** or an ice pack on the **neck** can help the blood vessels to contract.

Usually a nosebleed stops by itself after a few minutes. But if it bleeds for **a very long time** or **very heavily**, you need a doctor. This also applies if the nosebleed occurs after a hard fall on the head or comes back very often. Against dry air it helps, in winter, to air the room well and to care for the nose with an ointment.

gewusst: The place at the front of the nose that is prone to bleeding is called Little’s area, in medical Latin the Locus Kiesselbachi.
Even a little blood looks like a lot on a handkerchief.

teile.einleitung: Nail fungus is a condition in which fungi attack a fingernail or toenail. It is common and not dangerous to life, but stubborn, and treatment takes a lot of patience.
wichtigste: The technical term for nail fungus is onychomycosis.
Usually it is caused by thread fungi that feed on keratin.
Toenails are affected much more often than fingernails.
Fungi like damp warmth, for example in sweaty shoes.
You can catch it barefoot in indoor pools, saunas and showers.
Often athlete’s foot comes before nail fungus.
Treatment takes a long time, because the healthy nail has to grow back.

abschnitte.text: In nail fungus tiny **fungi** grow in the nail. Usually they are **thread fungi**. They feed on **keratin**, the horn that nails are made of. Less often yeasts or moulds are involved. The technical term is **onychomycosis**. It comes from Greek: “onyx” means nail, and “mykes” means fungus.

An affected nail usually turns **whitish to yellow-brown**. It becomes **thicker**, brittle and crumbly. Sometimes it even comes away from the nail bed. Usually the fungus begins at the front edge and spreads slowly. Whether it really is a fungus, a doctor can check with a small nail sample.

**Toenails** are affected much more often than fingernails. They are often in warm, damp **shoes** for a long time, and fungi love **damp warmth**. In addition toenails grow slowly. Often it all begins with **athlete’s foot** between the toes. If it is left untreated, the fungi can spread to the nails.

Fungal spores last well on **damp floors**, for example in the indoor pool, in the sauna or in showers. Anyone who walks barefoot there can pick them up. **Flip-flops** protect. It is also important to dry the feet and the **spaces between the toes** well after washing. Fresh socks every day and airy shoes make it hard for the fungi.

Against nail fungus there are special nail varnishes, creams and, in severe cases, tablets. But the affected part of the nail does not become healthy again. It has to be replaced by **healthy nail growing in**. Because toenails grow slowly, a treatment often takes **many months**. Anyone who stops too early risks the fungus coming back.

gewusst: Older people get nail fungus more often than children, because their nails grow more slowly.
Fungi belong neither to the plants nor to the animals, but form a kingdom of their own.

teile.einleitung: Mast cells are cells of the immune system that sit in the tissue. They are full of small granules containing messenger substances. They play an important part in allergies, for example in the itching after a mosquito bite.
wichtigste: Histamine is stored in the granules of mast cells.
Histamine causes itching and swelling.
Paul Ehrlich described mast cells in the late 19th century.
Their precursors are made in the bone marrow.
The release of the granules is called degranulation.
In mastocytosis, mast cells multiply abnormally.
The enzyme tryptase in the blood shows that mast cells have been activated.

abschnitte.text: The German scientist **Paul Ehrlich** described mast cells in the late **19th century**. Under the microscope they looked plump, because they contain many granules. People therefore took them for especially **well-fed cells**. In German, “mast” means fattening, and from this comes the name **mast cell**. The precursors of mast cells are made in the **bone marrow** and then mature in the tissue.

Mast cells are found mainly where the body comes into contact with the environment. These include the **skin**, the mucous membranes of the airways and the **intestine**. They often lie near small blood vessels. There they can react quickly when foreign substances or germs get in. They help, for example, in fighting parasites and in healing wounds.

In their granules, mast cells store messenger substances, above all **histamine**. When a mast cell is activated, it quickly releases the contents of the granules outwards. This is called **degranulation**. Histamine makes the blood vessels wider and more permeable. This causes **redness**, **swelling** and **itching**. In an **allergy**, mast cells react to substances that are really harmless, such as pollen.

In the rare **mastocytosis**, mast cells multiply abnormally and collect in the tissue. To prove mastocytosis or a strong activation of mast cells, the enzyme **tryptase** is measured in the blood. Against allergic complaints there are **antihistamines**, which block the effect of histamine. A **mast cell stabiliser** such as **cromoglicic acid**, on the other hand, already stops the release of histamine.

gewusst: The weal after a mosquito bite is partly a result of histamine from mast cells.
Paul Ehrlich received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1908 together with Ilya Mechnikov.

teile.einleitung: The emergency department is the ward in the hospital that you go to after an accident or a sudden serious illness. It is open day and night. Who is treated first depends on how urgent it is.
wichtigste: The emergency department is open around the clock, also at weekends.
You go there for accidents and sudden serious complaints.
Whoever is most seriously ill is treated first.
This sorting by urgency is called triage.
For minor complaints the family doctor’s practice is often the better place.

abschnitte.text: In every larger hospital there is an **emergency department**, often simply called “the emergency”. People come here after an accident, with strong pain, high fever or difficulty breathing. Some come themselves, and others are brought by the **ambulance**. Doctors and nurses are there around the clock.

In the emergency department it is not a case of first come, first served. On arrival a professional judges how urgent the case is. This is called **triage**. Whoever is **most seriously ill** or injured goes first. With a sprained foot you therefore sometimes have to wait a long time, so that people in danger of their life get help at once.

For minor complaints the **family doctor’s practice** or an emergency practice is often the right place. Many cantons also have a telephone number for medical advice. In danger of life in Switzerland you call **144** at once. In larger cities children are often treated in a **children’s emergency department** of their own.

gewusst: The word triage comes from French and means “selection” or “sorting”.
In the emergency department many different specialists work together, for example for bones, the heart and X-ray pictures.

teile.einleitung: A nerve cell is a specialised cell that can receive and pass on electrical signals. It is the most important building block of the brain, spinal cord and nerves. Without nerve cells you could neither think nor feel nor move.
wichtigste: The technical word for nerve cells is neurons.
Dendrites receive signals, and the axon passes them on away from the cell body.
At rest a nerve cell has a voltage of about -70 mV.
In the action potential sodium ions flow into the cell.
The myelin sheath around the axon speeds up conduction of the excitation.
Between the sections of myelin lie the nodes of Ranvier.
At the motor end plate acetylcholine passes the signal on to the muscle.

abschnitte.text: A nerve cell has a **cell body** with the cell nucleus. From it run many short, branched extensions, the **dendrites**, which receive signals. A long extension, the **axon**, passes the signals on away from the cell body. Some axons are over a metre long, for example from the spinal cord to the toes.

Even at rest a nerve cell is electrically charged, rather like a small battery. Inside it is negative compared with outside, and the **resting potential** is about -70 millivolts. This is provided by pumps in the cell membrane that carry sodium ions out and potassium ions in. These pumps use a great deal of energy.

If the cell is stimulated strongly enough, channels open and **sodium ions** flow into the cell. The inside briefly becomes positive, which is called depolarisation. After that potassium ions flow out and the voltage returns. This short burst of voltage is called an **action potential** and lasts only about a millisecond.

Many axons are surrounded by a fat-rich sheath, the **myelin sheath**. It insulates the axon like the plastic covering of a cable and speeds up conduction of the excitation greatly. Between the sections of myelin lie small, uninsulated gaps, the **nodes of Ranvier**. The signal jumps from node to node and so reaches over 100 metres per second.

At the end of the axon lies the synapse, where the signal is passed on to another cell. In this the nerve cell releases messenger substances, the **neurotransmitters**. At the motor end plate **acetylcholine** passes the signal from the nerve to the skeletal muscle. The muscle then contracts.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long extension that carries signals away from the cell body.
A short, branched extension that receives signals.
A short electrical impulse with which nerve cells pass on information.
An insulating cover around the axon that makes conduction faster.
A messenger substance that passes on signals at the synapse.

gewusst: The nodes of Ranvier are named after the French doctor Louis-Antoine Ranvier.
In the disease multiple sclerosis the myelin sheath is damaged, so signals are passed on more slowly or not at all.
Most nerve cells in the brain stay with you for life and no longer divide.

teile.einleitung: After lunch many people get tired. An **afternoon nap** can then give new strength. Small children need one almost every day, and adults sometimes treat themselves to a short nap.
wichtigste: An afternoon nap is a short sleep after lunch.
A short sleep during the day is also called a nap.
Small children most often need an afternoon nap.
Most children stop having one at about 3 to 5 years old.
For adults about 20 minutes is enough.
An afternoon nap that is too long makes it harder to fall asleep in the evening.
In Spain the midday rest is known as the siesta.

abschnitte.text: **Small children** need a great deal of sleep. The night alone is often not enough for them, so they usually sleep at midday too. Babies even sleep several times a day. In time children need less sleep during the day. Most stop having an afternoon nap between **3 and 5 years old**. Then the sleep at night is enough for them.

For adults a short **nap** of about 10 to 30 minutes is ideal, and often **20 minutes** is given. Such a nap refreshes you and helps you to be alert again. Anyone who sleeps longer falls into deep sleep and often wakes up groggy. In addition you are less tired in the evening, and **falling asleep** is harder. That is why an afternoon nap should not be too long and should not take place too late in the afternoon.

In some countries a midday rest is part of everyday life. Especially well known is the **siesta** in **Spain**. In the hot midday hours many people rest there, and some shops stay closed. The word comes from Latin and refers to the sixth hour of the day, that is, about midday. In other warm countries too, a break at midday is common.

For an afternoon nap, a **quiet, slightly dark room** is suitable. Quiet and little light help you to fall asleep, while noise and bright light keep you awake. A sofa or a comfortable armchair is often enough. In Switzerland many day nurseries have a rest room where the little ones can sleep after eating.

gewusst: The afternoon dip after lunch is also connected with our inner clock, not just with a full belly.
The German word for a nap, “Nickerchen”, comes from the fact that when you fall asleep sitting up, your head often nods forwards.

teile.einleitung: MRSA stands for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. This is a form of a common bacterium against which many antibiotics no longer work. Especially in hospitals, MRSA is a well-known problem.
wichtigste: Under the microscope, staphylococci look like balls in grape-shaped clusters.
Many healthy people carry Staphylococcus aureus in the front of the nose.
MRSA was first described in the 1960s.
The resistance to methicillin comes from the gene mecA.
Severe MRSA infections are often treated with vancomycin.
In hospital, consistent hand disinfection is the most important thing.

abschnitte.text: **Staphylococci** are ball-shaped bacteria. Under the microscope they often lie together in **grape-shaped clusters**. This is where the name comes from: the Greek word “staphyle” means grape. The species **Staphylococcus aureus** lives in many healthy people in the **front of the nose** or on the skin without making them ill. But if it gets into wounds or the blood, it can cause infections.

**Antibiotics** are medicines against bacteria. But some bacteria become **resistant**, which means that the medicine no longer works. **Methicillin** is an antibiotic from the penicillin group. Shortly after it was introduced, **MRSA** was first described in the **1960s**. The resistance comes from the gene **mecA**. It makes sure that many antibiotics of this group can no longer attack.

In **hospital** there are many weakened people, often with wounds or catheters. There, MRSA can become dangerous. It is passed on mainly through the **hands**. That is why **consistent hand disinfection** is the most important protective measure. Anyone who carries MRSA is often cared for in a room of their own, and the staff wear protective clothing.

Severe MRSA infections are often treated with the antibiotic **vancomycin**. There are also other drugs. Many people only carry MRSA without being ill. In them a **decolonisation** can be done: the bacteria are removed from the **skin and mucous membranes** with special ointments and washing solutions. To avoid resistance, antibiotics should be taken only when they are really needed.

gewusst: About one in three people carries Staphylococcus aureus in the nose, usually without noticing.
The name “aureus” means “golden”, because the bacteria form golden yellow colonies on culture plates.

teile.einleitung: A hospital-acquired infection, technically called a nosocomial infection, is an infection that you pick up in hospital or in a care home. The word comes from the Greek word for hospital. The most important means against it is good hand hygiene.
wichtigste: Nosocomial infections are acquired in hospital or in a care home.
An infection usually counts as nosocomial at the earliest about 48 hours after admission.
Urinary catheters raise the risk of urinary tract infections.
The WHO describes five moments for hand hygiene.
The hands should be rubbed with disinfectant for 20 to 30 seconds.
In Switzerland Swissnoso records hospital infections.

abschnitte.text: Many germs live in hospital, and many patients are weakened. That is why you can catch an infection there. If an infection appears at the earliest about **48 hours** after admission, it usually counts as **nosocomial**. If it was there before, you usually brought it with you from home. Common are infections of the urinary tract, lungs, wounds and blood.

In the **intensive care unit** the risk is especially high. There many people have **catheters**, tubes and a weakened **immune system**. Through such access points germs can easily get into the body. A **urinary catheter**, for example, raises the risk of a urinary tract infection greatly. That is why it is removed as soon as it is no longer needed.

As early as the 19th century the doctor **Ignaz Semmelweis** in Vienna recognised that washing hands saves lives. In 1847 he had doctors clean their hands with **chloride of lime**, and far fewer patients fell ill. Today the **WHO** describes five moments in which health staff should disinfect their hands, for example before and after contact with patients. The product is rubbed in for **20 to 30 seconds**.

The national centre **Swissnoso** records hospital infections and develops measures against them. The federal government has adopted the **NOSO strategy** for this. It sets out how hospital infections are monitored, prevented and fought. The careful use of antibiotics is part of it too.

gewusst: In his lifetime Semmelweis was not taken seriously by many colleagues. Only later did people realise how right he was.
Disinfecting the hands with alcohol is often kinder to the skin than frequent washing with soap.

teile.einleitung: An mRNA vaccine brings the cells a set of instructions for building a protein of a germ. The cells make this protein briefly, and the immune system gets to know it. Such vaccines became well known during the Covid-19 pandemic.
wichtigste: mRNA is a set of instructions for building a protein.
In the Covid-19 vaccine it is the blueprint for the spike protein.
The mRNA is read at the ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
It does not get into the cell nucleus and does not change the DNA.
Tiny fat envelopes, the lipid nanoparticles, protect the mRNA.
After a few days the cell breaks the mRNA down.

abschnitte.text: **mRNA** stands for messenger RNA. In every cell it carries blueprints from the genetic material to the protein factories. An mRNA vaccine against Covid-19 contains the blueprint for the **spike protein**. This is a protein on the surface of the coronavirus. The cells make this protein for a short time. The **immune system** recognises it as foreign and learns to fight it. If it later meets the real virus, it can react more quickly.

The vaccine mRNA stays in the **cytoplasm**, the inside of the cell outside the nucleus. There the **ribosomes** read it and build the protein. The mRNA does **not get into the cell nucleus** and does not change the DNA. mRNA is a short-lived molecule. After a few days the cell’s own enzymes break it down. What remains is the **immunological memory**.

Free mRNA would quickly break down in the body. That is why it is packed in tiny fat envelopes, the **lipid nanoparticles**. They protect the mRNA and fuse with the cell membrane. In this way the set of instructions gets into the cell. Because mRNA is delicate, the first Covid-19 vaccines had to be stored **deep-frozen**. The vaccine from Pfizer and BioNTech initially needed about **minus 70 degrees Celsius**. This made distribution difficult.

For a long time foreign mRNA caused too strong inflammation in the body. **Katalin Karikó** and **Drew Weissman** discovered that modified building blocks help. In the Covid-19 vaccines the building block **uridine** is replaced by a modified form, N1-methylpseudouridine. In this way the mRNA is recognised less as foreign, and more protein is made. For this work the two received the **Nobel Prize** in Physiology or Medicine in **2023**.

In Switzerland the authority **Swissmedic** checks whether a vaccine is safe and effective. In **December 2020** it approved the mRNA vaccine from Pfizer and BioNTech. It was the first Covid-19 vaccine approved in Switzerland.

gewusst: The idea of using mRNA as a medicine was being researched decades before the Covid-19 pandemic.
An mRNA vaccine does not contain a whole virus, only the blueprint for a single protein.

teile.einleitung: In almost every cell of our body, tiny **mitochondria** are at work. They are often called the “powerhouse of the cell”, because they obtain energy from nutrients.
wichtigste: Mitochondria are cell organelles and are regarded as the power stations of the cell.
Cell respiration takes place in them.
For this they need oxygen.
They make the energy carrier ATP.
A mitochondrion has two membranes, and the inner one is strongly folded.
The folds are called cristae.
According to the endosymbiont theory, mitochondria were once independent bacteria.

abschnitte.text: A **mitochondrion** is a **cell organelle**, that is, a small component with a particular job in the cell. Here energy is obtained from nutrients, hence the comparison with a power station. The energy is stored in the molecule **ATP** (adenosine triphosphate). ATP is the energy currency of the cell. Muscles need it, for example, to contract, and the brain needs it for thinking.

In the mitochondria, **cell respiration** takes place. In it, sugar is broken down step by step and energy is released. This needs **oxygen**. We breathe it in with the lungs, and the blood carries it to every cell. Without oxygen, mitochondria cannot break down sugar completely. Carbon dioxide and water are produced as waste, and we breathe the carbon dioxide out again.

A mitochondrion has **two membranes**, a smooth outer one and an inner one. The inner membrane is strongly folded. These folds are called **cristae**, which is Latin and means crests. The folds create a large surface. There sit the proteins that supply most of the energy for the cell.

Cells that need a lot of energy have especially many mitochondria. A good example is the **heart muscle cells**. The heart works without a break, day and night. A large part of its cell volume therefore consists of mitochondria. Muscle and nerve cells are also well equipped with them. Red blood cells, on the other hand, have none at all.

abschnitte.titel: Once living things of their own
abschnitte.text: The **endosymbiont theory** explains where mitochondria come from. A very long time ago, bacteria were taken in by larger cells. They were not digested but went on living inside and worked together with the cell. In time they became organelles. One clue to this is that mitochondria still have **their own DNA** today.

gewusst: Mitochondria have their own genetic material, separate from the genetic material in the cell nucleus.
Red blood cells have no mitochondria, so that they do not use up the oxygen themselves.

teile.einleitung: Nociceptors are the pain receptors of our body. They report to the brain when something could damage the body. Pain is unpleasant, but it protects us.
wichtigste: Pain receptors are called nociceptors in technical language.
Most are free nerve endings.
They react to strong heat, strong pressure and harmful substances.
Pain signals travel along nerve fibres of different speeds.
Endorphins are substances made by the body that dampen pain.
Anyone who feels no pain often does not notice injuries in time.

abschnitte.text: The name comes from the Latin word **nocere**, which means “to harm”. Nociceptors sit in the skin, in muscles, joints and many organs. Most are **free nerve endings**, that is, fine nerve ends without a special sheath. They react to **strong heat**, **strong pressure** and **harmful substances**, for example in inflammation.

After a knock you often feel first a **bright, stabbing** pain and shortly after a **dull** one. This is due to the nerve fibres. Thin fibres with a sheath, the **A-delta fibres**, conduct quickly. Even thinner fibres without a sheath, the **C fibres**, conduct slowly. This is how the signals arrive one after the other in the brain.

If you rub a place you have knocked, other nerves report a **touch**. These signals can dampen the passing on of the pain in the **spinal cord**. That is why it often hurts less afterwards. The body itself also has painkillers: in great exertion it makes **endorphins**, which ease pain.

abschnitte.titel: When pain is missing or stays
abschnitte.text: Some people feel **no pain from birth**. This sounds practical, but is dangerous. They often do not notice injuries or burns in time. The other way round there is **phantom pain**: people feel pain in a part of the body that is no longer there, for example after an amputation. This shows that pain arises in the brain.

gewusst: Chilli feels sharp and hot because the substance capsaicin irritates the same receptors as heat.
The brain itself has no pain receptors.

teile.einleitung: **Mineralocorticoids** are hormones from the adrenal cortex. They regulate how much salt and water the body keeps. The most important of them is **aldosterone**.
wichtigste: The most important mineralocorticoid in humans is aldosterone.
It is made in the adrenal cortex.
In the kidney, aldosterone takes sodium back and lets potassium be passed out.
With the sodium, the body also holds back water.
The enzyme renin from the kidney sets off the chain leading to the release of aldosterone.
ANP from the atria of the heart acts as its opponent.

abschnitte.text: The name says it: mineralocorticoids regulate the **minerals**, above all **sodium** and **potassium**. They are made in the outermost layer of the **adrenal cortex**. The most important is **aldosterone**. In the kidney it acts in the distal tubule and the collecting duct. There it makes sure that sodium is taken back into the blood and, in exchange, potassium is passed out in the urine. Because water follows sodium, more water stays in the body and blood pressure rises.

If the blood pressure in the kidney falls, it releases the enzyme **renin**. Renin starts a chain of steps that ends with **angiotensin II**. This substance narrows blood vessels and stimulates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone. Experts call the whole thing the **renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system**. It helps the body to keep blood pressure and blood volume steady.

If there is a lot of blood in the circulation, the **atria of the heart** are stretched. They then release the hormone **ANP**, the atrial natriuretic peptide. ANP inhibits the release of aldosterone. The kidney then passes out more sodium and water. In this way the heart itself puts on the brakes when there is too much fluid in the body.

In **Conn’s syndrome**, the adrenal cortex makes too much aldosterone. High blood pressure and a low potassium level are typical. In **Addison’s disease**, the adrenal cortex is usually destroyed by the body’s own immune system, and cortisol and aldosterone are missing. Then low blood pressure and a craving for salt can occur. As a replacement for aldosterone, **fludrocortisone** is given. The medicine **spironolactone**, on the other hand, blocks the aldosterone receptor and acts as a potassium-sparing diuretic.

gewusst: Without aldosterone the body would lose so much salt that blood pressure could fall dangerously.
Spironolactone is called potassium-sparing because sodium and water are passed out but potassium stays in the body.

teile.einleitung: The suprachiasmatic nucleus is the master clock of the body. It is a tiny group of nerve cells in the brain and sets the daily rhythm. It makes sure that we become tired in the evening and awake in the morning.
wichtigste: The suprachiasmatic nucleus lies in the hypothalamus above the optic chiasm.
It receives information about light from the retina through the retinohypothalamic tract.
The photopigment melanopsin reports the light to the inner clock.
The proteins CLOCK and BMAL1 switch on the clock genes Per and Cry.
It coordinates the peripheral clocks in organs such as the liver and heart.
Without it the sleep-wake rhythm loses its daily order.

abschnitte.text: The name describes the position: **supra** means “above”, and the **optic chiasm** is the **crossing of the optic nerves**, where the optic nerves of both eyes meet. The nucleus therefore lies directly above it in the **hypothalamus**, a small part of the diencephalon. It consists of two tiny halves, left and right.

The inner clock does not run exactly 24 hours. That is why it is reset every day by light. In the retina there are special **ganglion cells** with the photopigment **melanopsin**. They report the brightness along a pathway of their own, the **retinohypothalamic tract**, to the suprachiasmatic nucleus. This controls, among other things, when the pineal gland makes the sleep hormone **melatonin**.

In the clock cells a chain of genes and proteins is at work. The proteins **CLOCK** and **BMAL1** together form a complex. It switches on the clock genes **Per** and **Cry**. Their proteins later inhibit CLOCK and BMAL1 again. This creates a loop that lasts about a day. Even single cells in a **cell culture** keep a daily rhythm of their own.

If the nucleus is destroyed in experimental animals, the **sleep-wake rhythm** loses its daily order. The animals then sleep spread over day and night. In **hamsters** without a master clock of their own, the nucleus of another animal was put in. The animals then took on the **rhythm of the donor animal**. The nucleus also coordinates the **peripheral clocks** in organs such as the liver or heart.

gewusst: The Nobel Prize in Medicine was awarded in 2017 for the discovery of how the inner clock works at the level of genes.
Even blind people can often still report light to their inner clock if the melanopsin cells work.

teile.einleitung: Marcel Hug is one of the most successful wheelchair athletes in the world. The Swiss has been winning big races on the track and on the road for many years. His nickname is “Silver Bullet”.
wichtigste: Marcel Hug is a Swiss wheelchair track and road athlete.
He comes from the canton of Thurgau.
His nickname is “Silver Bullet”.
He has won several gold medals at the Paralympic Games.
He has won many big marathons, for example in Boston, London and Berlin.

abschnitte.text: **Marcel Hug** was born in 1986 and grew up in the **canton of Thurgau**. He has used a **wheelchair** since birth and began wheelchair sport as a child. He races over short and long distances, from the track to the **marathon**. At the **Paralympic Games** he has won several gold medals, for example in Rio de Janeiro in 2016 and in Tokyo in 2021.

He got his nickname **“Silver Bullet”** because of his **silver helmet**. The name also fits because he is very fast in his racing wheelchair. At big marathons such as those in **Boston**, **London**, **Berlin** or **New York** he has often stood at the top of the podium.

A **racing wheelchair** looks quite different from an everyday wheelchair. It has three wheels and is built long and low. It is driven with the arms, using push rims on the wheels. For this you need a great deal of **strength** and **stamina** in the arms, shoulders and trunk. In **Nottwil** in the canton of Lucerne stands the Swiss Paraplegic Centre, where many wheelchair athletes train.

gewusst: Marcel Hug has been named Swiss Disabled Sportsperson of the Year several times.

teile.einleitung: A neuron is the technical word for a nerve cell that passes on electrical signals in the nervous system. Neurons are the cells with which you think, feel, remember and move. They form huge networks that are more complex than any computer.
wichtigste: Neurons are the cells that pass on electrical signals in the nervous system.
The human brain contains about 86 billion neurons.
A neuron can be connected to thousands of other neurons.
Sensory neurons report stimuli, and motor neurons control muscles.
Neurons pass on their signals at synapses with messenger substances.
In learning, connections between neurons are strengthened.
Besides neurons there are glial cells, which support and supply them.
