abschnitte.text: The word **neuron** comes from Greek and means sinew or nerve. A neuron consists of a cell body, dendrites and an axon. The dendrites take in signals, and the axon passes them on. This creates a chain along which information travels through the body.

**Sensory neurons** report stimuli from the eyes, ears or skin to the brain. **Motor neurons** send orders to the muscles. In between lie interneurons, which link and process information. Most neurons in the brain are such interneurons.

The human brain has about 86 billion neurons. Each can be connected through **synapses** to thousands of others. Together this gives an unimaginable number of connections, and estimates speak of over 100 trillion. This network makes thinking, language and memory possible.

When you practise something often, for example riding a bike or the times tables, certain connections between neurons become stronger. This ability is called **plasticity**. Unused connections, on the other hand, become weaker with time. That is why regular repetition is worthwhile in learning.

At the end of the 19th century the Spaniard **Santiago Ramón y Cajal** studied neurons under the microscope. He showed that the nervous system consists of single cells. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1906, together with the Italian Camillo Golgi. His drawings of neurons are admired to this day.

begriffe.erklaerung: A nerve cell that passes on electrical signals.
A connection point between two neurons.
The ability of the brain to change through learning.
A helper cell that supports, protects and feeds neurons.

gewusst: Artificial neural networks, the basis of many computer programs with artificial intelligence, are named after neurons.
The cerebellum contains more neurons than the whole rest of the brain together.
Even a baby is born with almost all the neurons it will need later.

teile.einleitung: Muscles are the motors of our body. Without them we could neither move an arm nor run, breathe or smile. A muscle works by contracting and pulling on bones as it does so.
wichtigste: Muscles move the body by contracting.
There are skeletal, heart and smooth muscles.
A tendon joins a muscle to a bone.
Muscles can only pull, not push, so every skeletal muscle needs an opposing muscle.
The biceps bends the arm, and the triceps straightens it.
On the inside a skeletal muscle consists of bundles of muscle fibres.
Regular exercise makes muscles stronger.
Muscle pain the day after a lot of sport is called sore muscles.

abschnitte.text: A **muscle** is a tissue that can contract. Humans have over 600 skeletal muscles, which together can make up almost half of body weight. When a muscle works, it becomes shorter and thicker. In doing so it uses energy from food and produces heat, which is why we get warm when doing sport.

A skeletal muscle is built from many **muscle fibres** that are gathered into bundles, rather like threads in a rope. Each fibre is a long cell that can be up to several centimetres long. Inside lie tiny protein threads that slide into one another when the muscle contracts. At both ends the muscle turns into a **tendon**, which fixes it to the bone.

The **skeletal muscles** move arms, legs and the whole body, and they obey our will. The **smooth muscles** are found in the stomach, intestine, bladder and blood vessels and work by themselves. The **heart muscle** pumps blood for a whole life without ever getting tired. Only the skeletal muscles can we control consciously.

Muscles can only pull, not push. That is why they work in pairs: the **biceps** at the front of the upper arm bends the arm, and the **triceps** at the back straightens it again. While one contracts, the other relaxes. The muscles at the front and back of the thigh work in a similar way, for example.

Through regular exercise muscle fibres become thicker and stronger, and the muscle becomes more enduring. Anyone who does not move, on the other hand, loses muscle strength, for example after weeks in a plaster cast. After unaccustomed effort tiny tears appear in the fibres, which hurt the next day. That is **sore muscles**. They heal by themselves after a few days.

Muscles need **protein** from foods such as dairy products, eggs, fish, meat or pulses. Warming up before sport protects against strains. Enough sleep is important, because muscles recover and grow during rest. Stretching also keeps the muscles supple.

begriffe.erklaerung: A firm band that joins a muscle to a bone.
A long muscle cell that can contract.
A muscle that carries out the opposite movement.
Muscle pain after unaccustomed effort.

gewusst: The largest muscle of the human body is the gluteus maximus, and one of the smallest sits in the ear on the stirrup bone.
For a smile you need only a few muscles in the face, and altogether there are over 40 muscles in the face.
The heart is a muscle that beats about three billion times in a lifetime.

teile.einleitung: In the knee joint lie two crescent-shaped discs of cartilage, the menisci. They cushion shocks and make sure the knee is stable. In sports with a lot of twisting they can be injured.
wichtigste: A meniscus consists of fibrous cartilage.
The Greek word means “little moon”.
The menisci lie between the thigh bone and the shin bone.
They cushion and spread the pressure over a larger area.
The inner meniscus tears much more often than the outer one.
A tear often happens when twisting on a bent knee that is bearing weight.
Surgery is mostly done with keyhole surgery of the joint.

abschnitte.text: The name **meniscus** comes from Greek and means **“little moon”**. The menisci have the shape of a crescent moon. In each knee there are two: the **inner meniscus** and the **outer meniscus**. They lie between the **thigh bone** and the **shin bone**. They consist of **fibrous cartilage**, a firm but still slightly elastic tissue.

The joint surfaces of the thigh and shin do not fit together exactly. The menisci make up for this. They **cushion shocks**, for example when jumping and running. They also **enlarge the contact surface** and **spread the pressure** more evenly. This protects the cartilage of the joint. In addition the menisci make the knee more stable.

A meniscus tears especially easily when **twisting on a bent knee that is bearing weight**. This happens in football, skiing or tennis, for example. The **inner meniscus** tears **much more often**, because it is more firmly joined to the inner ligament and is therefore less mobile. In older people a meniscus can also tear through wear, sometimes with just a simple movement.

After a tear the knee often hurts when bending or twisting, and it can swell. If a torn piece gets caught in the joint, the knee suddenly **cannot be straightened completely**. This is then called a locked joint. To investigate, an **MRI** is often done, in which the menisci can be seen well.

Not every tear has to be operated on. When surgery is done, today it is mostly with **keyhole surgery of the joint**, **arthroscopy**. In this, a camera and fine instruments are put into the knee through small cuts. A tear in the outer edge can often be stitched. In the **inner part**, however, a tear **heals badly**, because this part has **hardly any blood supply**. There, often only the damaged piece is removed.

gewusst: The jaw joint also has a disc of cartilage that works rather like a meniscus.
Doctors today try to keep as much of the meniscus as possible, because it protects the knee in the long term.

teile.einleitung: The sodium-potassium pump is a protein in the cell membrane that transports ions against their gradient. It makes sure that there are different amounts of sodium and potassium inside and outside the cell.
wichtigste: The pump sits in the cell membrane.
In each cycle it brings three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in.
The energy comes from splitting ATP.
During the cycle the pump protein is phosphorylated.
The alpha subunit carries the binding sites for ATP and ions.
Jens Christian Skou received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1997 for its discovery.
Cardiac glycosides inhibit the pump and are used in heart failure.

abschnitte.text: The sodium-potassium pump is a **transmembrane protein**. It crosses the **cell membrane** and so joins the inside of the cell to the space outside. Only there can it transport ions to and fro. The pump consists of subunits. The large **alpha subunit** is the working part: it binds ATP, sodium and potassium. The smaller **beta subunit** helps mainly with correct building into the membrane.

The pump is an **ATPase**: it gets its energy from **splitting ATP**. In this a phosphate group is briefly bound to the pump protein. This is called being **phosphorylated**. As a result it changes its shape and opens alternately inwards and outwards. In each cycle it brings **three sodium ions out** and **two potassium ions in**. Because one net positive charge goes out, the pump is called **electrogenic**.

Because of the pump there is a lot of potassium inside and a lot of sodium outside. These **ion gradients** are the basis for the **resting potential** and the **action potential** of nerve cells. For a single action potential the pump is not directly needed, though. Only a few ions flow in it. The pump restores the concentrations over a longer time. If it is blocked, the gradients slowly run down through leak currents.

The Dane **Jens Christian Skou** described the enzyme in 1957 in the nerves of **crabs**. In 1997 he received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry** for it. In medicine **cardiac glycosides** such as digoxin play a part. They originally come from the **foxglove** and inhibit the pump in heart muscle cells. This indirectly raises the calcium in the cell, and the heart beats more strongly.

gewusst: A large part of the energy the brain uses goes to the sodium-potassium pump.
The foxglove is a poisonous plant from which heart medicines have been obtained.

teile.einleitung: The nocebo effect is the opposite of the placebo effect. If a person expects something bad, they can really get complaints, even without an active substance. It shows how strongly thoughts influence the body.
wichtigste: “Nocebo” is Latin and means “I shall harm”.
The positive counterpart is the placebo effect.
The main causes are expectation and conditioning.
The nocebo effect is especially well researched in pain.
Careful communication about risks can reduce it.

abschnitte.text: The Latin word **nocebo** means “I shall harm”. The counterpart **placebo** means “I shall please”. In the nocebo effect the **expectation** of something bad triggers real complaints, such as a headache, sickness or tiredness. A second reason is **conditioning**: the body has learned to react to a certain situation with complaints.

Many people read in the **leaflet** of a medicine which side effects are possible. Afterwards they suddenly notice these complaints in themselves. Part of this comes not from the active substance, but from the expectation. In **pain**, too, this is well researched: anyone who believes that something will hurt often feels stronger pain.

In medical studies one group gets the real medicine and another a **dummy medicine** without an active substance. In this placebo group too, many people complain of side effects. Since they have received no active substance at all, this is a **nocebo effect**. Such results help us to understand which complaints really come from the medicine.

Doctors have to inform people honestly about risks. How they do it, though, makes a difference. **Balanced communication** also says how many people have no side effects. In this way nocebo effects can be reduced without hiding anything.

gewusst: The nocebo effect can even lead people to stop a medicine although it would actually help them.
Even the way an injection is announced can influence how strongly you feel the prick.

teile.einleitung: Neuroplasticity means that the brain can change throughout life. Connections between nerve cells become stronger or weaker, depending on how we use them.
wichtigste: Neuroplasticity is the ability of the brain to rebuild itself.
Donald Hebb described in 1949 that neurons that are active at the same time strengthen their connection.
Long-term potentiation is a long-lasting strengthening of a synapse.
It was described in 1973 in the hippocampus.
The NMDA receptor plays a key role in it.
Long-term depression weakens synapses.
In the dentate gyrus new nerve cells arise even in adults.

abschnitte.text: In 1949 the researcher **Donald Hebb** set out an important rule in his book “The Organization of Behavior”. If two nerve cells are **active at the same time**, their connection becomes stronger. Later this was often summed up in the English sentence “cells that fire together, wire together”. This idea helps to explain why **practising** achieves something: connections that are used often are strengthened.

If a **synapse** is stimulated intensely, the cell after it reacts more strongly for hours to weeks afterwards. This is called **long-term potentiation**, LTP for short. Timothy Bliss and Terje Lømo described it in 1973 at synapses in the **hippocampus** of rabbits. This region of the brain is important for forming new memories. A key role is played by the **NMDA receptor**. It opens only when glutamate binds and the cell is excited at the same time. Then calcium flows in and starts the strengthening.

Synapses can also become lastingly **weaker**. This is called **long-term depression**, LTD for short. The word here does not mean an illness. Strengthening and weakening together allow the brain to adjust its networks finely. For a long time people believed that the adult brain made no new nerve cells. Today we know that new neurons arise in the **dentate gyrus**, a part of the hippocampus. How strong this is in humans is still being researched.

In development there are windows of time in which the brain is especially malleable for certain experiences. These are called **critical periods**. The researchers **Hubel and Wiesel** showed: if one eye is covered in an early phase, it can later hardly use the visual cortex any more. There are similar windows of time, for example, for **learning languages**. That is why children often find pronunciation easier than adults.

In the cerebral cortex there is a kind of **map of the body** on which every part of the body has its area. If an arm or leg is missing after an **amputation**, neighbouring areas take over the area that has become free. This reorganisation is linked with **phantom pain**. In it people affected feel pain in a part of the body that is no longer there at all.

gewusst: David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1981 for their research on seeing.
Even in old age the brain can still learn new things and adapt.

teile.einleitung: Dairy products are made from milk. They include cheese, yoghurt, quark, butter and cream. In Switzerland they have a long tradition, and many specialities are world-famous.
wichtigste: Quark, yoghurt, cheese, butter and cream are dairy products.
In Switzerland most milk comes from cows.
In Switzerland the German word for cream is “Rahm” rather than “Sahne”.
If cream is whipped for a very long time, butter is made.
In cheese-making, yellowish whey is left over.
Emmental is known for its big holes.
Opened milk belongs in the fridge.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland most milk comes from **cows**. There is also milk from goats and sheep. Many farms keep dairy cows, and in summer many animals graze in the **Alps**. Milk contains protein, fat, milk sugar and **calcium**, which is important for the bones. Many different **dairy products** are made from it.

Dairy products include **yoghurt**, **quark**, **cheese**, **butter** and **cream**. In Switzerland people say **Rahm** for cream, and in Germany rather Sahne. To make yoghurt, certain bacteria are added to the milk, which make it thick and slightly sour. If you whip cream, it first becomes whipped cream. If you keep whipping for **a very long time**, the fat separates off, and **butter** is made.

In **cheese-making**, the milk is curdled with rennet or bacteria. Then the mass is cut up. In this, the solid cheese mass separates from a yellowish liquid, the **whey**. The cheese mass is pressed into moulds, salted and then often matures for months in a cellar. Whey is used, for example, as a drink or animal feed.

Switzerland is known for its cheese. **Emmental** has **big holes**. They arise from gases that bacteria make during ripening. Other well-known kinds are Gruyère, Appenzeller and Sbrinz. A popular dish is **fondue**: melted cheese is put on the table in a shared pot, the caquelon. You dip pieces of bread into it with long forks.

Dairy products are delicate and go off quickly when it is warm. **Opened milk** therefore belongs in the **fridge** and should be drunk soon. Yoghurt, quark and cream are also kept cool. Hard cheese keeps longer because it contains little water. The packaging shows how long a product will keep at least.

gewusst: For one kilogram of Emmental you need about 12 litres of milk.
In Switzerland there are several hundred different kinds of cheese.

teile.einleitung: The Nutri-Score is a coloured label on food packaging. It shows at a glance how balanced the make-up of a product is. This makes it easier to compare similar products when shopping.
wichtigste: The Nutri-Score has five levels from A to E.
Level A is dark green, and level E is red.
It was developed in France and introduced there first.
It is calculated per 100 g or 100 ml.
In Switzerland it is voluntary.
It is most useful for comparing similar products.

abschnitte.text: The Nutri-Score consists of **five levels** with the letters **A to E**. **A** is **dark green** and stands for a rather favourable make-up. Then follow light green, yellow, orange and finally **red for E**. The letter of the product is shown larger on the packaging.

The calculation always relates to **100 g or 100 ml**. There are minus points for a lot of **energy**, **sugar**, **saturated fats** and **salt**. There are plus points for **fibre**, protein and for shares of fruit, vegetables and nuts. The level results from the total.

The Nutri-Score was developed by experts in **France** and introduced there in 2017. Later other countries took it on, for example Belgium and Germany. In **Switzerland** it is **voluntary**: the manufacturers decide for themselves whether they print it on the packaging. The Federal Food Safety and Veterinary Office supports it as a voluntary aid.

The Nutri-Score is best suited to comparing **similar products**, such as two muesli mixes or two yoghurts. A comparison between olive oil and cola, on the other hand, makes little sense. Critics complain that it does not take into account the **degree of processing** and **additives**. Supporters think that it still offers simple guidance.

gewusst: The calculation of the Nutri-Score is revised by experts again and again so that it becomes more accurate.
Even a product with an A should not be eaten in any amount you like.

teile.einleitung: Myosin is a protein that works like a tiny motor. Together with the protein actin it makes sure that our muscles can contract.
wichtigste: Myosin is a motor protein that turns energy from ATP into movement.
One molecule of myosin II has two heavy and four light chains.
The myosin head binds actin and splits ATP.
The links between myosin heads and actin are called cross bridges.
The myosin heads pull the actin filaments towards the middle of the sarcomere.
Myosin V transports cargo such as vesicles through the cell.
Without ATP the heads stay stuck to the actin: this explains rigor mortis.

abschnitte.text: The myosin in muscle is called **myosin II**. One molecule consists of two **heavy chains** and four **light chains**. The heavy chains form two heads and a long, twisted tail. Many tails lie together and form the **thick filaments** in the muscle. The **myosin head** is a motor and an enzyme at the same time: it binds actin and splits ATP.

In muscle work the myosin head attaches to an actin filament. This creates a **cross bridge**. Then the head lets go of the phosphate that arose when ATP was split. This **release of the phosphate** triggers the power stroke: the head tilts and pulls the actin a little further. A new ATP releases the head again, and the cycle starts over. Each round uses up one ATP.

A muscle is divided into many small units, the **sarcomeres**. The myosin heads on both sides pull the actin filaments towards the **middle of the sarcomere**. As a result the Z discs at the edge move closer together, and the muscle becomes shorter. The filaments themselves do not shorten in the process, they slide past each other. This **sliding filament theory** was published in 1954 in two papers in the journal “Nature”.

There are many different classes of myosin. **Myosin V** has two heads and walks with them step by step along actin filaments. In doing so it pulls cargo such as **vesicles** and organelles through the cell. Other motor proteins such as kinesin and dynein, on the other hand, walk on microtubules.

After death the body no longer makes ATP. Without ATP the myosin heads can no longer let go of the actin. The muscles therefore stay firmly joined and become stiff. This is called **rigor mortis**. It only goes away when the proteins are broken down after some time.

gewusst: The sliding filament theory comes from two pairs of researchers: Andrew Huxley with Rolf Niedergerke and Hugh Huxley with Jean Hanson.
The two researchers called Huxley were not related to each other, despite the same name.

teile.einleitung: Anaesthesia makes sure that during an operation you sleep deeply and feel no pain. Thanks to anaesthesia, even big operations are possible today.
wichtigste: In general anaesthesia you sleep deeply and feel nothing.
The anaesthetist is responsible for the anaesthesia.
Before an anaesthetic you have to stay without food for a few hours.
Children often breathe in the anaesthetic through a mask.
During the operation heartbeat and breathing are monitored.
You wake up in the recovery room.
Afterwards you are often still tired and a little dazed.

abschnitte.text: In **general anaesthesia** you are put into a deep, artificial sleep with medicines. You feel **no pain** and notice nothing of the operation. There is also **local anaesthesia**. In it only a part of the body goes numb, and you stay awake, for example at the dentist.

The specialist doctor for anaesthetics is called an **anaesthetist**. She gives the **anaesthetic** and stays nearby during the whole operation. Machines constantly show how the **heart** is beating and how well you are **breathing**. In this way she notices at once if something is not right and can react.

Before an anaesthetic you have to be **fasting**. That means: not eating anything for a few hours. During the anaesthetic the protective reflexes do not work as usual. That way no food can get from the stomach into the **lungs**. Children often get the anaesthetic through a **breathing mask** that they breathe in. Sometimes it also flows through a thin tube into a **vein**.

After the operation you go to the **recovery room**. There you are watched carefully until you are fully awake again. The anaesthetic needs some time until it has left the body. That is why you often still feel **tired and dazed**. Some people also feel a little sick. After that you go to the patient’s room or may go home.

In earlier times operations were done without proper numbing, which was very painful. In 1846 the dentist **William Morton** showed an anaesthetic with **ether** in public in Boston. This is regarded as the beginning of modern anaesthesia. Since then the drugs have become much safer and easier to control.

gewusst: The German word “Narkose” comes from the Greek “narkosis”, which means numbness.
Most people remember nothing of the operation after an anaesthetic.

teile.einleitung: Muscles consist of different **muscle fibre types**. Some fibres are slow and enduring, others fast and strong but quick to tire. The mixture helps to decide whether someone is more likely to run a marathon or to sprint.
wichtigste: Type I fibres are slow and enduring.
Type IIx fibres contract fastest and tire most quickly.
Type IIa fibres lie in between and work oxidatively and glycolytically.
Myoglobin gives type I fibres their red colour.
Marathon runners usually have many type I fibres in their legs.
Classically the types are told apart by the activity of myosin ATPase.

abschnitte.text: **Type I fibres** contract slowly but hardly tire. They are also called **slow-twitch fibres**. They get their energy **oxidatively**, that is, with oxygen. That is why they have many mitochondria and are surrounded by especially many **capillaries**, which make short routes for the oxygen. Their red colour comes from **myoglobin**, a pigment that stores oxygen in the muscle.

**Type IIa fibres** are fast and **oxidative and glycolytic**. They can get energy both with and without oxygen and so lie between type I and type IIx. **Type IIx fibres** contract fastest. They get their energy mainly **glycolytically**, that is, from the quick breakdown of sugar without oxygen. In return they tire after a short time. Because they contain little myoglobin, they look paler.

Classically the fibre types are told apart **histochemically**, that is, by staining tissue samples. What matters is the activity of **myosin ATPase**. Different forms of myosin split ATP at different speeds. This speed also decides how quickly the fibre contracts.

**Marathon runners** often have clearly more than half type I fibres in their leg muscles. **Sprinters**, on the other hand, have many fast type II fibres. In a movement the fibres are used according to the **size principle**, which is also called Henneman’s principle. First small motor units with slow fibres work. Only when a lot of force is needed do the large, fast units join in.

gewusst: The dark meat of a chicken leg contains more enduring red fibres than the pale breast.
How many fast and slow fibres someone has depends strongly on their inherited traits.

teile.einleitung: Tiredness is a sign from the body: it needs a break and sleep. Someone who is tired finds it harder to concentrate and reacts more slowly.
wichtigste: Tiredness shows that the body and brain need rest.
Heavy eyes and frequent yawning are typical.
Only real sleep helps against tiredness.
The hormone melatonin makes us tired in the evening.
Too little sleep makes you unable to concentrate and in a bad mood.
Caffeine, for example in cola, can disturb falling asleep.
Anyone who rides a bike when tired reacts more slowly.

abschnitte.text: When the body needs sleep, the **eyelids become heavy** and almost close by themselves. You yawn often, rub your eyes and have less strength. Many people also become **irritable** and in a bad mood. Anyone who wakes up fit in the morning and stays lively during the day has usually had enough sleep.

In the evening, when it gets dark, the body makes the hormone **melatonin**. It tells the body that it is now time for sleep. Bright light, especially from screens, can slow the production of melatonin. That is why it is good to put your phone and tablet away before sleeping. A dark, quiet room helps you to fall asleep.

A tired **brain** works more slowly. You find it harder to pay attention and remember less. In sleep the brain sorts out what you have learned during the day. Children of school age therefore need a lot of sleep, usually about 9 to 11 hours a night. Regular bedtimes help the body to get into a good rhythm.

Someone who is very tired **reacts more slowly** and overlooks dangers more easily. In road traffic, for example on a bike, this can lead to accidents. Adults too should not drive tired. When you are very tired, only a break or sleep helps, not a trick.

Drinks such as coffee, cola or energy drinks contain **caffeine**. Caffeine keeps you awake for a while but does not replace sleep. It can disturb falling asleep and is not suitable for children. Much better against tiredness are enough sleep, exercise in the fresh air and drinking enough water.

gewusst: Yawning is catching: if you see someone yawn, you often have to yawn yourself.
While you sleep, not only the muscles but also the brain recover.

teile.einleitung: A scar is the place where a wound has healed. The body repairs the skin with new tissue that looks a little different from the skin next to it.
wichtigste: A scar arises when a wound heals.
Mainly deep wounds leave scars.
Fresh scars are often reddish.
With time scars usually become paler and flatter.
Hair usually does not grow on scars.
You protect fresh scars from the sun.
A scar usually stays for life.

abschnitte.text: When you injure yourself, the body begins **wound healing** straight away. First the wound closes with blood and a scab. Underneath, the body makes new **tissue**. With small scratches the skin grows back almost exactly the same. With **deep wounds** this does not work. Then the body fills the gap with firm **scar tissue**.

A **fresh scar** has a good blood supply and therefore looks **reddish**. Over the months it gets less blood. It becomes **paler and flatter**. In scar tissue **hair roots** and sweat glands are missing. That is why hair usually does not grow on a scar. A scar can no longer disappear completely, and it usually stays visible for life.

A deep cut heals better if a doctor **stitches** or glues it. In this the **edges of the wound** are held together. Then only a narrow scar remains. You should not pick at the **scab**, because this disturbs healing. Clean wounds heal faster and more nicely than inflamed ones.

Fresh scar tissue reacts sensitively to **sunlight**. Without protection it can **turn brownish**, and the scar stands out more. That is why you cover fresh scars with clothes or a plaster, or protect them with sun cream. Sometimes a scar grows into a thick ridge, and this is called a **raised scar**. In such cases a skin doctor helps.

gewusst: Scar tissue is less stretchy than normal skin.
Scars can also arise on inner organs, for example after an operation.

teile.einleitung: The lymphatic system is a fine network of vessels and organs that runs through the whole body. It carries tissue fluid back into the blood and supports the body’s defence. The lymph nodes that you can sometimes feel in your neck during a cold belong to it.
wichtigste: The lymphatic system carries tissue fluid and supports the immune defence.
The liquid in the lymph vessels is called lymph.
Lymph nodes filter the lymph and hold germs back.
The spleen, thymus and tonsils also belong to the lymphatic system.
Many lymphocytes, a kind of white blood cell, live in the lymph.
The lymphatic system has no heart of its own, and the lymph is pushed along by muscle movements.
Swollen lymph nodes often show that the body is fighting an infection.

abschnitte.text: A little liquid constantly seeps out of the fine blood vessels into the tissue to supply the cells. Most of it flows back into the blood, but some stays between the cells. The **lymph vessels** collect this tissue fluid, and then it is called **lymph**. It is pale and slightly yellowish and contains many defence cells.

Lymph vessels begin very fine in the tissue and join up into ever larger vessels. The largest is the thoracic duct, which leads the lymph into a large vein near the neck. In this way the liquid returns to the blood. Valves in the vessels make sure that the lymph flows in one direction only.

On its way the lymph flows through **lymph nodes**, small bean-shaped filter stations. Humans have several hundred of them, especially many in the neck, the armpits, the groin and the belly. In the lymph nodes, **lymphocytes** wait for germs and fight them. In an infection the lymph nodes swell, because the defence cells multiply strongly there.

Besides the lymph nodes, other organs belong to the lymphatic system. The **spleen** in the upper left of the belly filters the blood. In the **thymus** behind the breastbone, the T lymphocytes mature in children. The tonsils in the throat catch germs that get in through the mouth and nose.

In the intestine the lymphatic system has a special job. Fat from food is not taken up straight into the blood, but first into the lymph vessels of the intestinal villi. After a fatty meal the lymph there therefore looks milky white. This is also where the German name for the thoracic duct, “milk-chest duct”, comes from.

The lymphatic system has no pump of its own like the heart. The lymph is pushed along by the movement of the muscles and by breathing. That is why your feet can swell after sitting or standing for a long time. If the lymph backs up for good, a **lymphoedema** develops, which is treated with a special massage, lymphatic drainage.

begriffe.erklaerung: A pale liquid that flows in the lymph vessels.
A small filter station in which defence cells fight germs.
A white blood cell that fights germs in a targeted way.
A swelling caused by too much liquid in the tissue.

gewusst: About two to three litres of lymph flow back into the blood every day.
In a sore throat the doctor often feels the lymph nodes in the neck, because they are then swollen.
Movement is important for the flow of lymph, because the muscles push the lymph along like a pump.

teile.einleitung: Myelin is a fat-rich protective layer that wraps around many nerve fibres like the insulation of an electric cable. This sheath is called the myelin sheath. It makes sure that nerve signals race through the body much faster.
wichtigste: Myelin is a fat-rich substance that wraps around nerve fibres.
The protective layer around the nerve fibres is called the myelin sheath.
The myelin sheath speeds up the transmission of signals greatly.
It works rather like the insulation around an electric cable.
Between the sections of myelin lie small gaps, the nodes of Ranvier.
In the brain myelin forms the white matter.
In the disease multiple sclerosis myelin is damaged.

abschnitte.text: **Myelin** consists of about three quarters fats and one quarter proteins. It is made by special cells that wind several times in a spiral around a nerve fibre. This creates the **myelin sheath**, a thick, insulating cover. Because it has a whitish shine, areas with many such fibres are called white matter.

Nerves pass on information as electrical signals, for example from the finger to the brain. Without myelin the signal travels slowly, bit by bit along the fibre. With myelin it jumps from gap to gap, the **nodes of Ranvier**. As a result signals become up to a hundred times faster, and some nerves conduct over 100 metres per second.

You can imagine a nerve fibre with a myelin sheath as an **insulated cable**. The insulation prevents the signal from being lost on the way. In this way even a very long nerve fibre, for example from the back to the toes, can pass on signals reliably. In the brain, oligodendrocytes make the myelin, and in the nerves of the body the Schwann cells do.

At birth many nerve fibres are hardly wrapped in myelin yet. **Myelination** advances strongly in childhood and youth. That is why babies only gradually learn to hold up their head, to grasp and to walk. In the frontal lobe, which is important for planning and self-control, this process lasts until young adulthood.

In **multiple sclerosis**, MS for short, the body’s own immune system attacks the myelin sheaths in the brain and spinal cord. As a result nerve signals are disturbed or slowed. People affected can have, for example, problems with their sight, tingling, paralysis or great tiredness. In Switzerland over 15000 people live with MS. It cannot yet be cured, but it can be treated well.

begriffe.erklaerung: The long extension of a nerve cell that passes on signals.
An insulating cover of myelin around a nerve fibre.
A small gap in the myelin sheath over which the signal jumps.
The part of the brain and spinal cord with many myelinated fibres.

gewusst: The white matter makes up about half of the human brain.
Anyone who practises an instrument can strengthen the myelin layer in certain areas of the brain.
Thanks to myelin a signal from the foot reaches the brain in a fraction of a second.

teile.einleitung: An oedema is a swelling because fluid collects in the tissue. It often appears at the ankles and lower legs. Oedemas can be harmless, but can also point to an illness.
wichtigste: An oedema is a build-up of water in the tissue.
The ankles and lower legs often swell.
A finger pressed on it often leaves a dent.
Heart failure can lead to oedemas in the legs.
A pulmonary oedema is an emergency.
Water tablets help to flush water out.

abschnitte.text: In our body some fluid constantly flows out of the fine blood vessels into the tissue and back again. If this balance is thrown out, fluid collects **between the cells**. The place swells. This is called an **oedema**. If you press the swelling with a finger, the fluid is pushed away. Often a **dent** then remains, which stays visible for a while.

Because of **gravity**, fluid collects easily in the lower part of the legs. That is why the **ankles** often swell, especially after standing or sitting for a long time. On **hot summer days** the blood vessels widen. Then more fluid escapes into the tissue, and the feet become fatter. Raising the legs and movement often help.

Sometimes an illness is behind it. If the heart pumps too weakly, blood backs up in the veins. In such **heart failure** oedemas often appear in the legs. If fluid collects in the air sacs of the lungs, this is called a **pulmonary oedema**. The people affected find it hard to breathe. This is an **emergency**.

Besides the blood vessels there are the **lymph vessels**. They carry away tissue fluid, the **lymph**. If this drainage is disturbed, a **lymphoedema** arises. A special massage, **lymphatic drainage**, can help. For many oedemas doctors prescribe **water tablets**, also called diuretics. They make the kidneys pass out more water and salt.

gewusst: The word oedema comes from Greek and means “swelling”.
A mosquito bite also swells, because fluid collects in the tissue at that spot.

teile.einleitung: 144 is the emergency number for medical emergencies in Switzerland. Anyone who dials it reaches an emergency call centre, which sends the ambulance service. The call is always free.
wichtigste: On 144 you reach the ambulance service.
The number is there for medical emergencies.
The call costs nothing.
The most important thing is to say where the accident is.
The person in the emergency call centre ends the call.
You must never call 144 for fun.

abschnitte.text: **144** is there for **medical emergencies**. That means when someone is seriously injured, unconscious, not breathing properly or suddenly has very strong pain. In the **emergency call centre** trained professionals work. They send the **ambulance service**, that is, an ambulance with paramedics and, if needed, an emergency doctor too.

Most important is the **place**: where is the accident? Give the street, house number or a place that is easy to find. Then you say what has happened and how many people are injured. The professional asks questions, and you answer calmly. **Do not hang up.** The call is always ended by the **person in the emergency call centre**. Sometimes they even explain on the phone how you can help.

In Switzerland there are several numbers: **117** for the **police**, **118** for the **fire brigade** when something is burning, and **145** for **Tox Info Suisse** when someone has swallowed something poisonous. **1414** alerts Rega. The European emergency number **112** also works. All emergency calls are **free**.

You must **never call 144 for fun**. Every false call blocks the line for people who really need help. Anyone who raises a false alarm on purpose can be punished. If you are unsure whether it is an emergency, you may still call. The professionals help you to decide.

gewusst: If you forget the numbers: 112 works in the whole of Europe.
The emergency call centre can stay in contact with the ambulance and describe the way to it.

teile.einleitung: A height chart hangs on the wall in many children’s rooms or kitchens. You can read off how tall you are. With marks and dates you can even see how quickly you are growing.
wichtigste: With a height chart you measure body height.
You stand in front of it barefoot and straight.
A book or a board laid flat on the head shows the exact height.
The zero of the height chart must be at the floor.
100 centimetres are 1 metre.
A centimetre has 10 millimetres.

abschnitte.text: A **height chart** is a long strip of wood, paper or plastic with a **centimetre scale**. You fix it upright on the wall. For it to measure correctly, the **zero must be exactly at the floor**. If it hangs too high or too low, none of the numbers are right. So when you hang it, it is best to check with a metre rule.

For an exact measurement you stand **barefoot** and **straight** with your back to the wall. Heels, bottom and the back of the head touch the wall, and you look straight ahead. A second person lays a **book** or a **board** flat on the head so that it touches the wall. Where the book touches the height chart, they make a mark. This way hair or a crooked look does not show a wrong value.

On the height chart there are mostly **centimetres**. **100 centimetres** are exactly **1 metre**. If a mark is at 100 cm, the child is 1 metre tall. Between two centimetres you often see even smaller marks. These are **millimetres**, and **1 centimetre has 10 millimetres**. This way you can read it off very precisely.

Next to each mark you often write the **date** and the name. This way you can see later **when you were that tall**. An example: Leo’s mark last year was at **110 cm**, and today it is at **117 cm**. So Leo has grown **7 cm**. Children do not always grow at the same speed, and sometimes there are real growth spurts.

gewusst: In the morning you are slightly taller than in the evening, because the discs in the back are pressed together a little during the day.
Doctors enter children’s heights on growth charts to follow their development.

teile.einleitung: Sneezing is a protective reflex with which the body blows dust, pollen or germs out of the nose. A strong blast of air shoots through the nose and mouth. Sneezing happens quite automatically, and you can hardly suppress it.
wichtigste: Sneezing is a reflex that you do not control consciously.
If dust gets into the nose, the body wants to blow it out quickly.
Sneezing is triggered by irritated nerves in the nasal lining.
When sneezing the eyes almost always close.
Sneezing spreads many tiny droplets.
You should sneeze into the crook of your arm to protect others.
Bright light can also trigger sneezing in some people.

abschnitte.text: Sneezing is a **reflex**, that is, an automatic reaction of the body. If dust, pollen or pepper irritate the nasal lining, the body wants to blow the troublemakers out quickly. First you breathe in deeply, then the air is pushed out with great force. This frees the nose again.

In the nasal lining sit fine nerve endings. If they are irritated, they send a signal to the **sneezing centre** in the brainstem. This triggers a precisely coordinated movement of the chest, stomach and neck muscles. The eyelids too almost always close in the process.

In a cold you often sneeze, because viruses irritate the nasal lining. When sneezing, thousands of tiny **droplets** fly through the air. In them there can be germs that infect others. That is why you should sneeze into the **crook of your arm** or into a handkerchief.

Many people in Switzerland sneeze especially often in spring and summer. The cause is an **allergy** to pollen from trees, grasses or flowers, hay fever. The body wrongly takes the harmless pollen to be dangerous. Besides sneezing, watering eyes and a runny nose are typical.

Some people have to sneeze when they suddenly look into bright sunlight. This is called the **photic sneeze reflex**, and it is inherited. Cold air, a full stomach or plucking the eyebrows can also trigger sneezing in some people. Why this is so has not yet been fully researched.

begriffe.erklaerung: An automatic reaction of the body without thinking.
Moist skin inside the nose that catches dust.
An exaggerated defence reaction of the body to harmless substances.
Infection through tiny drops when sneezing, coughing or speaking.

gewusst: You do not normally sneeze in your sleep, because the nerves then react less sensitively.
Sneezing with your eyes open is almost impossible.
Many cultures have a wish that is said after a sneeze, and in German people say “Gesundheit”, which means “health”.

teile.einleitung: After a tiring day of sport the muscles sometimes hurt, often only the next morning. That is **sore muscles**. They are unpleasant but harmless and go away by themselves.
wichtigste: You usually feel sore muscles on the next day or the day after.
They arise from tiny tears in the muscle fibres.
Mainly unaccustomed or very tiring movements set them off.
They usually last a few days.
Rest and light movement help.
Sore muscles are not dangerous.
If you repeat an exercise regularly, they get weaker.

abschnitte.text: If a muscle has to do something **unaccustomed** or very tiring, **tiny tears** appear in the muscle fibres. The body repairs these small injuries, and the tissue swells slightly as it does so. This hurts for a while. Sore muscles arise exactly in the muscles that have worked. After lots of sit-ups you therefore feel them in the **stomach**, and after a long bike ride more in the legs.

Sore muscles usually begin only **hours after the sport**. You often feel them most strongly on the next day or the day after. After **a few days** they are usually gone again, at the latest after about a week. Sore muscles are **not dangerous**, and the muscle heals by itself. Strong pain right during the sport, on the other hand, is more likely a sign of an injury.

You get sore muscles especially easily when the muscle has to **brake**. A good example is a hike **steeply downhill**. With every step the thighs have to catch the body. This braking work puts the fibres under heavy strain. Anyone who walks a long descent in the Swiss mountains often notices this clearly the next day.

Above all the muscle needs **time** to heal. **Rest** and relaxed movement, such as a walk, do many people good. A **warm bath** can also be pleasant. You should only do hard exercise again when the pain has gone. Anyone who repeats a new exercise every week usually gets **less and less** sore muscle, because the muscle gets used to it.

gewusst: It used to be believed that lactic acid in the muscle was to blame for sore muscles, but this is now considered disproved.
Even a single training session protects the muscle for some time from getting severe sore muscles again with the same exercise.

teile.einleitung: Neurotransmitters are chemical messenger substances with which nerve cells pass on signals. They jump from one cell to the next at a small point of contact, the synapse. Without them we could neither think nor move.
wichtigste: Neurotransmitters pass on signals at chemical synapses.
They are released into the narrow synaptic cleft.
Calcium gives the starting signal for the release.
Glutamate is the most important exciting messenger substance in the brain.
GABA is the most important brake in the brain, and glycine inhibits mainly in the spinal cord.
The sympathetic system works on the organs mostly through noradrenaline.

abschnitte.text: A nerve cell passes a signal on as an electrical impulse, the **action potential**. At the end of the cell lies the **terminal bouton**. There channels open, and **calcium** flows into the cell. This makes small sacs, the **vesicles**, fuse with the cell membrane. Special proteins, the **SNARE proteins**, help with this.

The vesicles give their messenger substance into the **synaptic cleft**, a tiny space between two cells. The substance travels across to the next cell and binds there to **receptors**. These fit the messenger substance like a lock fits a key. After that the messenger substance is broken down or taken up again, so that the signal stays short.

Some messenger substances make the next cell more active. They produce a small change in voltage, the **EPSP** (excitatory postsynaptic potential). If enough of them come together, the cell itself fires. The most important exciting substance in the brain is **glutamate**. Braking is done mainly with **GABA** and, in the spinal cord, with **glycine**. These open channels for chloride and make the cell harder to excite.

**Acetylcholine** controls the muscles. **Noradrenaline** is released by the **sympathetic system**, the part of the nervous system that puts the body on alert. It raises the pulse, for example. **Dopamine** plays a part in movement and reward, and **serotonin** in mood and sleep. A special case is the gas **nitric oxide**, which is not stored in vesicles.

Many poisons attack synapses. **Botulinum toxin** cuts up the SNARE proteins and so prevents release. **Strychnine** blocks the receptors for glycine, which leads to cramps. Many medicines also work at synapses, for example sedatives that strengthen the effect of GABA.

gewusst: The pharmacologist Otto Loewi showed in 1921, using frogs’ hearts, that nerves pass on signals chemically. For this he received the Nobel Prize in 1936.
Nitric oxide can even travel backwards from the next cell to the sending cell.

teile.einleitung: In a kidney transplant a person whose kidneys no longer work receives a donated kidney. It is the most common organ transplant in the world. Afterwards the person usually no longer needs dialysis.
wichtigste: A kidney transplant is the putting in of a donated kidney.
The kidney is the organ transplanted most often in the world.
The first successful kidney transplant took place in 1954.
A healthy person can donate a kidney during their lifetime.
Medicines prevent the body from rejecting the new kidney.
In Switzerland the foundation Swisstransplant coordinates organ donation.

abschnitte.text: The new kidney is usually put into the **lower abdomen**, near the pelvis. Doctors connect it to blood vessels and to the bladder. The person’s own diseased kidneys usually stay in the body, because removing them would be an unnecessary risk. Often the new kidney starts to make urine soon after the operation.

Donor kidneys come from people who have died or from **living donors**. Because you can live well with **one** healthy kidney, parents, brothers and sisters or friends, for example, can donate a kidney. The donation is voluntary and is thoroughly checked beforehand.

The **immune system** recognises the new kidney as foreign and wants to fight it. That is why people who have had a transplant take **immunosuppressants** for the rest of their lives. These are medicines that dampen the defences. As a result, though, they are a little more prone to infections and have to go for regular check-ups.

In Switzerland the national foundation **Swisstransplant** distributes donor organs fairly according to fixed rules. In 2022 the voters accepted the **extended presumed consent rule**. Under it, anyone who does not expressly object may be considered as a donor, with relatives being involved.

gewusst: The first successful kidney transplant in 1954 in Boston took place between identical twins, because their bodies do not reject each other’s tissue.
A donated kidney from a living person often works for many years.

teile.einleitung: Lymph nodes are small organs spread all over the body. They filter the lymph and help the body to fight off germs. In a cold you can sometimes feel them in your neck.
wichtigste: Lymph nodes belong to the lymphatic system.
The lymph is filtered in them.
The lymph vessels carry the lymph to the lymph nodes.
An adult has about 600 lymph nodes.
Lymph nodes are bean-shaped and contain many lymphocytes.
In an infection they swell, because defence cells multiply strongly there.

abschnitte.text: **Lymph nodes** are small, **bean-shaped** organs. Most are only a few millimetres to about a centimetre across. An adult has about **600** of them. Many lie in the **neck**, in the armpits, in the groin and in the belly. They belong to the **lymphatic system**, a network of vessels and organs that helps with defence.

Besides blood, **lymph**, a pale liquid, also flows through the body. It is collected by the **lymph vessels** and carried to the lymph nodes. There it is **filtered**. Germs, dead cells and foreign substances get caught. Then the lymph flows on and finally reaches the blood.

In the lymph nodes there are particularly many **lymphocytes**. These are defence cells, a kind of white blood cell. When they meet germs, they recognise them and **multiply strongly**. That is why lymph nodes often **swell** in an infection and can be sore to the touch. In a cold you can often feel them well in the **neck**.

Swollen lymph nodes in a cold or sore throat are usually harmless. They get smaller again when the illness is over. But if they stay big for a long time without your being ill, or if they are very hard, you should have this checked by a doctor. That is why doctors often feel the lymph nodes during an examination.

gewusst: The tonsils in the throat also belong to the lymphatic system.
The spleen is the largest organ of the lymphatic system.

teile.einleitung: For us to move, for the heart to beat and for food to travel through the intestine, we need **muscle tissue**. There are three kinds: skeletal muscle, heart muscle and smooth muscle.
wichtigste: There are skeletal muscle, heart muscle and smooth muscle.
Heart muscle is striated but works involuntarily.
In contraction actin and myosin slide past each other.
Calcium ions from the sarcoplasmic reticulum trigger the contraction.
ATP releases the myosin heads from the actin again.
The messenger substance at the motor end plate is acetylcholine.

abschnitte.text: The **skeletal muscle** moves the bones and can be controlled at will. Under the microscope it shows cross striping. The **heart muscle** is also **striated**, but works **involuntarily**. It is steered by a system of its own that produces the excitation. The **smooth muscle** is found, for example, in the intestine, blood vessels and bladder. It has no cross striping and also works by itself.

In contraction the protein threads **actin** and **myosin** slide past each other. The myosin heads pull on the actin filaments and push them towards each other. In this way the muscle shortens without the filaments themselves becoming shorter. The trigger is **calcium ions** from the **sarcoplasmic reticulum**, a store in the muscle cell. Calcium binds to troponin and frees the binding sites on the actin. For the heads to let go again, **ATP** is needed.

Every voluntary movement begins with a signal from a nerve. The point of contact between a motor nerve fibre and a skeletal muscle fibre is called the **motor end plate**. There the messenger substance **acetylcholine** is released. It binds to receptors in the muscle membrane and opens ion channels. The arrow poison **curare** blocks these receptors and in this way paralyses the muscles.

**Skeletal muscle fibres** have many cell nuclei. They arise during development when many single-nucleus precursor cells, the **myoblasts**, fuse with each other. Such a structure is called a **syncytium**. Heart muscle cells, on the other hand, are joined by **intercalated discs**. These contain adhesive junctions and gap junctions, small channels through which the excitation spreads quickly from cell to cell.

gewusst: After death ATP is missing, so actin and myosin no longer let go and the muscles become firm in rigor mortis.
Thanks to its own pacemaker, the heart keeps beating even if the nerves to the heart are cut.

teile.einleitung: An emergency doctor is a doctor who comes directly to the scene of an accident or to a serious emergency. In this way treatment begins before the injured person is in hospital. Emergency doctors ride in the ambulance or fly in the helicopter.
wichtigste: Emergency doctors come directly to the accident or emergency.
They travel in the ambulance or fly in the rescue helicopter.
They work closely with paramedics.
In Switzerland they are alerted through the emergency number 144.
Rega flies with emergency doctors on board, also into the mountains.

abschnitte.titel: Help at the scene of the accident
abschnitte.text: In a serious accident every minute counts. That is why not only the **ambulance service** but, if needed, also an **emergency doctor** comes to the scene. They examine the injured person, give medicines against pain and make sure that breathing and circulation are working. Only when the condition is stable enough does the person go to hospital.

Often the emergency doctor drives to the call in a vehicle of their own or in the **ambulance**. In remote areas and in the mountains they come by **rescue helicopter**. In Switzerland, for example, **Rega**, the Swiss air rescue service, flies with a doctor on board. Its number is **1414**.

Emergency doctors have studied medicine and afterwards completed additional training in **emergency medicine**. They work in a team with **paramedics**, who are also well trained. Everyone is alerted through the emergency call centre with the number **144**. The centre decides whether an emergency doctor is needed.

gewusst: Rega was founded in 1952 and is funded to a large part by donors.
A rescue helicopter can also reach places that no car can drive to.

teile.einleitung: Earwax is a yellowish, sticky mass in the ear canal. It may not look nice, but it is very useful. It protects and cleans the ear quite by itself.
wichtigste: Earwax is made in the outer ear canal.
It protects the ear from dirt and germs.
Normally it travels outwards by itself.
Cotton buds push the earwax deeper in.
It is enough to wash the outside of the pinna.
A hard plug is best removed by a doctor.

abschnitte.text: In the **ear canal**, the passage from the ear inwards, there are small glands. Together with dead flakes of skin they make **earwax**. Experts call it **cerumen**. It keeps the skin in the ear canal supple, catches **dirt** and dust and protects against germs.

The earwax **travels outwards by itself**. On the way it takes dirt with it. Chewing and speaking help, because the ear canal moves slightly as you do so. That is why you do not need to clean the ear canal. It is enough to clean the **outside of the pinna** with a cloth when washing.

You should not put **cotton buds** deep into the ear. They **push the earwax deeper in** instead of getting it out. There it can become lodged. You can also injure the ear canal or the sensitive **eardrum**.

Sometimes too much earwax collects and forms a **plug**. Then you **hear less well**, and the ear feels muffled. A hard plug is best removed by a **doctor**. Often she first gives **special ear drops** that make the hard wax soft. Then she carefully flushes out the ear.

gewusst: There are two kinds of earwax, wet and dry. Which kind you have is inherited.
In East Asia especially many people have dry earwax.

teile.einleitung: **Minerals** are vital substances that the body cannot make itself. We take them in with food and drink. They build bones and teeth and help nerves and muscles to work.
wichtigste: Minerals have to be taken in with food.
The body needs bulk elements such as calcium in larger amounts, and trace elements only in tiny traces.
Calcium is the main building block of bones and teeth.
Vitamin D helps the gut to take up calcium.
Table salt is sodium chloride, and the WHO recommends less than 5 g a day.
Magnesium is important for muscles and nerves.
When you sweat, you lose mainly sodium.

abschnitte.text: Minerals are divided into two groups. **Bulk elements** such as calcium, magnesium, sodium, potassium and chloride occur in the body in larger amounts. **Trace elements** such as iron, iodine, zinc or fluoride are needed only in tiny traces. Both groups are important. Because the body cannot make minerals itself, we have to take them in with **food**. A varied diet usually supplies enough of them.

**Calcium** makes bones and teeth hard and firm. Good sources are milk and dairy products such as cheese and yoghurt, but also some mineral waters and green vegetables. So that the gut can take up calcium well, it needs **vitamin D**. Our skin makes this vitamin with the help of sunlight. Calcium also helps with muscle work and blood clotting.

Table salt consists chemically of **sodium** and **chloride**, and its formula is NaCl. Sodium regulates the water balance and helps to pass on nerve signals. The **World Health Organization** recommends adults less than **5 g of salt** a day, about one teaspoon. In Switzerland people eat clearly more on average, often hidden in bread, cheese or ready meals. When you sweat, the body loses sodium, which is why sweat tastes salty.

**Magnesium** plays a part in muscle relaxation and the conduction of nerves. Many people take it for cramps in the calves. It is found in nuts, wholegrain and green vegetables. Green leafy vegetables such as spinach contain a lot of it, because every **chlorophyll** molecule carries a magnesium atom in its centre. The trace element **iron** is important for the red blood pigment that carries oxygen.

gewusst: As early as 1922 Switzerland introduced iodised table salt, to fight goitre, which was common at the time.
Without the magnesium in chlorophyll, plant leaves would not be green.

teile.einleitung: Nerves are like cables that carry messages through the whole body. They join the brain to muscles, skin and organs.
wichtigste: Nerves carry signals between the brain and the body.
The brain and nerves consist of nerve cells, also called neurons.
The spinal cord is the thick strand of nerves in the back.
The vertebrae protect the spinal cord.
Nerves in the skin report warmth, cold, pressure and pain.
The brain has about 86 billion nerve cells.
A pinched nerve makes a leg go to sleep.

abschnitte.text: **Nerves** carry signals through the body, rather as **cables** carry electricity. They bring messages from the skin and the sense organs to the brain. And they bring orders from the brain to the **muscles**. Nerves consist of many **nerve cells**, which experts call **neurons**. They can receive signals and pass them on in a flash.

The control centre is the **brain**. According to researchers’ estimates it has about **86 billion** nerve cells. From the brain the **spinal cord** runs down the back. This thick strand of nerves joins the brain to the nerves in the whole body. It lies protected in a canal through the **vertebrae** of the spine.

In the **skin** there are many nerve endings. They report to the brain whether something is **hot or cold**, whether you are being touched or whether something hurts. **Pain** is a warning signal: if you touch a hot hob, you pull your hand back in a flash. This is how the nervous system protects the body from injuries.

abschnitte.titel: Tingling and legs gone to sleep
abschnitte.text: At the elbow a nerve lies very close under the skin. If you knock yourself there, at the so-called **funny bone**, the nerve is directly irritated, and there is a strong tingling as far as the fingers. If you sit on one leg for a long time, nerves are **pressed together**. They then conduct badly for a short time, and the leg “goes to sleep”. When you move it again, it tingles until everything works normally.

The word nerve also occurs in sayings. If someone says “That gets on my nerves”, they mean: **that annoys me**. Someone who has “good nerves” stays calm even in difficult situations. And someone who “loses their nerves” gets very upset.

gewusst: The longest nerve of the body is the sciatic nerve, which reaches from the back to the foot.
Some nerve signals travel at over 100 metres per second.

teile.einleitung: The spleen is a soft organ the size of a fist in the upper left of the belly. It filters old blood cells out of the blood and supports the immune system in fighting germs. Although it is important, in an emergency you can also live without a spleen.
wichtigste: The spleen lies in the upper left of the belly behind the lower ribs.
It filters old and damaged red blood cells out of the blood.
The spleen supports the immune system and belongs to the lymphatic system.
Many white blood cells live in it that fight germs in the blood.
A healthy spleen is about as big as a fist and weighs around 150 grams.
In a serious accident the spleen can rupture and bleed heavily.
You can live without a spleen but are more prone to certain infections.

abschnitte.text: The **spleen** lies at the top left of the belly, between the stomach and the diaphragm, protected by the lower ribs. It is dark red, soft and about 11 centimetres long. In adults it weighs about 150 grams. Because it has a very good blood supply, a lot of blood constantly flows through it.

Red blood cells live for about 120 days, and then they become old and stiff. In the spleen they have to squeeze through very narrow gaps. Old, stiff cells get stuck and are broken down by **eating cells**. The iron from them is reused to make new red blood cells.

The spleen is the largest organ of the **lymphatic system**. In its inside, the white pulp, sit many **lymphocytes**. They recognise bacteria and other germs in the blood and make antibodies against them. In this way the spleen catches invaders that have got straight into the blood.

In an unborn child the spleen itself makes **blood cells** for a time. After birth the bone marrow takes over this job. Later, however, the spleen still stores platelets and a small reserve of blood cells. In some animals such as the horse, it can release a lot of stored blood during exertion.

abschnitte.titel: A ruptured spleen and life without a spleen
abschnitte.text: In a heavy blow to the belly, for example in a cycling or skiing accident, the spleen can rupture. A **ruptured spleen** is dangerous because it bleeds heavily into the belly. Sometimes the spleen then has to be removed by surgery. Without a spleen the liver and lymph nodes take over some of its jobs, but people affected should make sure they are vaccinated especially well.

Many people know the **stitch** when running, often on the left or right side. In the past people believed that it came from the spleen tightening during sport. Today we know that the exact cause has still not been clearly established. It probably has to do with the diaphragm and the ligaments in the belly.

begriffe.erklaerung: An organ in the upper left of the belly that filters blood and helps with defence.
The soft inner tissue of the spleen.
A defence cell that swallows old cells and germs.
A network of vessels and organs that carries tissue fluid and defends the body.

gewusst: The spleen filters about one twentieth of all the blood every minute.
Some people have one or more small extra spleens besides the spleen.
In glandular fever the spleen can swell greatly, so people who are ill should not do contact sport for a while.

teile.einleitung: The nail bed is the skin under the fingernail or toenail. The hard nail plate lies on it, and its pink colour shimmers through the plate.
wichtigste: The nail bed is the skin on which the nail plate rests.
It has a good blood supply, so a healthy nail shimmers pink.
The nail plate is made in the nail matrix at the base of the nail.
The cuticle protects the nail matrix from germs.
A fingernail grows back completely in about 6 months.
Toenails grow much more slowly than fingernails.
You cut toenails straight so that they do not grow in.

abschnitte.text: A nail consists of several parts. The hard **nail plate** is made of horn, more exactly of the protein **keratin**. It lies firmly on the **nail bed**. At the base of the nail, hidden under the skin, lies the **nail matrix**. There new cells arise, which become horny and slowly push the nail plate forwards. The pale half moon at the base of the nail is the visible part of the matrix.

The nail plate is almost **transparent**. Beneath it lies the nail bed with many fine **blood vessels**. Their red colour shimmers through, and so a healthy nail looks pink. If the blood carries too little oxygen, for example in strong cold, it is darker. Then the nails shimmer **bluish**.

At the base of the nail a thin **cuticle** grows onto the nail. It seals the gap between skin and nail. In this way fewer germs reach the sensitive nail matrix. You should therefore not cut the cuticle, but at most push it back gently.

Nails grow slowly but steadily. Until a whole **fingernail** is renewed, about **6 months** go by. **Toenails** grow only about half as fast. A whole toenail needs about one to one and a half years. You cut toenails **straight**. If you cut the corners round, the nail can grow sideways into the skin: an **ingrown nail** arises and can become inflamed.

If you trap a finger hard, fine vessels in the nail bed can burst. The blood collects under the nail plate. A **bruise** arises, which shows through dark red to black. Often the dark spot slowly grows out with the nail. With strong pain a doctor can help.

gewusst: Nails consist of the same substance as hair: keratin.
On the finger you use most, the nail often grows a little faster.

teile.einleitung: Magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI for short, is a method with which doctors can look inside the body without opening it. It produces very detailed cross-section images. For this it needs a strong magnetic field and radio waves.
wichtigste: MRI produces images using a strong magnetic field and radio waves.
It is also called nuclear magnetic resonance imaging.
It does not use X-rays.
Soft tissues such as the brain, ligaments and cartilage can be seen especially well.
The strength of the magnetic field is measured in tesla.
Metal objects have to be taken off beforehand.
During the examination you hear loud knocking noises.

abschnitte.text: Our body consists largely of **water**. Water contains **hydrogen atoms**. Their nuclei behave like tiny magnets. In the strong **magnetic field** of the machine they line up. Then the machine sends **radio waves** into the body. The atomic nuclei then send weak signals back, and a computer works out cross-section images from them.

abschnitte.titel: What you can see with it
abschnitte.text: MRI is especially suitable for **soft tissues**. With it you can show the **brain**, the spinal cord, muscles, **ligaments** and **cartilage** very precisely. That is why it is often used after sports injuries to the knee or for headaches. A big advantage over computed tomography (CT) is that MRI uses **no X-rays**.

You lie on a couch that slides into a narrow tube. During the scans you have to lie as still as possible. The machine makes loud **knocking and humming noises**, so you are often given headphones or earplugs. Beforehand, all **metal objects** have to be taken off, such as jewellery, hair slides or keys. This is because the strong magnetic field pulls metal very powerfully.

The strength of a magnetic field is measured in **tesla**. Many machines in hospitals work with 1.5 or 3 tesla. That is much stronger than a fridge magnet. So that the magnet can be so strong, in many machines it is cooled to a very low temperature with liquid helium. The unit tesla is named after the inventor **Nikola Tesla**.

The chemist **Richard Ernst** of **ETH Zurich** received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in **1991**. He had developed methods of **nuclear magnetic resonance** that are also important for MRI. That is why the process is also called **nuclear magnetic resonance imaging**. In 2003 Paul Lauterbur and Peter Mansfield received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for their work on imaging with MRI.

gewusst: An MRI magnet is switched on even when nobody is being examined.
With MRI you can even see which areas of the brain are especially active at that moment.

teile.einleitung: When we breathe through the nose, the air is cleaned, moistened and warmed before it reaches the lungs. At the same time we can smell with the nose.
wichtigste: Nose hairs hold back dust and small particles.
Mucus in the nose catches dust and germs.
The moist nasal lining moistens dry air.
The nasal septum separates the two nostrils.
At the top of the nose sit the smell cells.
With a cold the nose is blocked, and you smell less well.
If dust tickles the nose, we sneeze.

abschnitte.text: When you breathe in, the air flows through the two **nostrils** into the nasal cavity. In the middle stands the **nasal septum**, a thin wall of cartilage and bone. It divides the nose into two halves. From the nose the air goes on into the throat, the windpipe and finally into the **lungs**.

The nose is a good **filter**. The **nose hairs** work like a sieve and hold back larger particles. In addition the nose constantly makes some **mucus**. **Dust and germs** stick to it. If dust tickles the nose, we **sneeze**: the air is pushed out powerfully, and the dust flies out again.

The **nasal lining** is moist and has a good blood supply. If dry, cold air flows through, it takes up **moisture** and **warmth**. This way the air reaches the lungs more comfortably and is kinder to them. This is an advantage over breathing through the mouth. Nasal breathing is therefore regarded as the natural and healthier way to breathe.

At the very top of the nose sit the **smell cells**. With the air we breathe in, **scent substances** reach them. That is why we can smell while breathing. The nose also helps when eating: a large part of the taste we actually notice through smell.

With a **cold** the nasal lining swells, and a lot of mucus forms. Then hardly any air gets through the nose, and we breathe through the **mouth**. Smelling gets worse too, because the scent substances hardly reach the smell cells. By **blowing your nose** you free the nose of mucus: you blow air firmly through the nose into a handkerchief.

gewusst: When you have a cold, food often tastes bland, because the smell is missing.
The nose often works in turns: sometimes more air flows through one nostril, sometimes through the other.

teile.einleitung: Negative feedback is a principle of control: an effect slows down its own cause. This is how the body keeps important values such as blood sugar or amounts of hormones in a healthy range.
wichtigste: In negative feedback the result acts back on the trigger to inhibit it.
A sensor measures the actual value and reports it to the controller.
A disturbance pushes the actual value away from the set value.
A lot of thyroxine inhibits the release of TRH and TSH.
Rising blood sugar leads to more insulin, and falling blood sugar to less.
Cortisone has to be tapered off slowly after long treatment.
Blood clotting is an example of positive feedback.

abschnitte.text: A **control loop** keeps a value as constant as possible, for example body temperature. The wanted value is called the **set value**, the actual one the **actual value**. A **sensor** or measuring element measures the actual value and reports it to the **controller**. A **disturbance**, for example cold, changes the value from outside. The controller evens out the difference. In **negative feedback** a rising value slows its own cause.

The **hypothalamus** makes TRH, which prompts the **pituitary gland** to release **TSH**. TSH prompts the **thyroid gland** to make thyroxine. If there is enough **thyroxine** in the blood, it inhibits TRH and TSH. The thyroid gland is stimulated less. In an **overactive thyroid** the thyroid gland itself makes too much hormone. Then TSH is low although thyroxine is high.

If **blood sugar** rises after eating, the pancreas releases more **insulin**. Insulin helps the cells to take up sugar, and blood sugar falls. If the sugar falls, less insulin is released too. This is a typical negative feedback.

The stress hormone **cortisol** is also controlled in this way: CRH and **ACTH** prompt the **adrenal cortex**, and cortisol inhibits them again. If someone takes **cortisone** as a medicine for a long time, it inhibits CRH and ACTH, and the body itself makes little cortisol. That is why such a treatment is **tapered off** slowly. If, the other way round, the adrenal cortex is destroyed, the inhibition is missing, and ACTH **rises strongly**. Because ACTH also stimulates the pigment cells, the skin often becomes darker.

In **positive feedback** a process reinforces itself. One example is **blood clotting**. Clotting factors that are made activate further factors until the wound is closed quickly. Such processes run briefly and strongly. For balance in the body, though, it is mainly negative feedback that is important.

gewusst: A thermostat on a heater works on the same principle as negative feedback in the body.
The balance that the body keeps in this way is called homeostasis.

teile.einleitung: Our body grows and heals because cells divide. In **mitosis** the cell nucleus divides so that two daughter cells with exactly the same genetic material arise.
wichtigste: Mitosis is the division of the cell nucleus.
Its phases are called prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.
In anaphase the sister chromatids are pulled to the poles of the cell.
The spindle fibres attach to the kinetochore.
The sister chromatids are joined together at the centromere.
After the division of the nucleus comes cytokinesis, the division of the cytoplasm.

abschnitte.text: Before a cell divides, it doubles its genetic material. After this, each chromosome consists of two identical halves, the **sister chromatids**. They are joined together at a narrowed spot, the **centromere**. A ring-shaped protein complex called **cohesin** holds them tightly enclosed. Mitosis itself runs in four classic phases: **prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase**.

In **prophase** the chromatin condenses strongly. The chromosomes thereby become visible as threads in the **light microscope**. At the same time the **spindle apparatus** forms from fine tubes, the microtubules. The spindle fibres bind to the **kinetochore**, a protein complex at the centromere. In **metaphase** all the chromosomes line up in the middle of the cell in one plane.

At the start of **anaphase**, the enzyme **separase** splits the cohesin. Only now can the sister chromatids come apart from each other. The spindle fibres pull them to the opposite **poles of the cell**. In this way each side gets a complete set of chromosomes. This step has to run very precisely, so that no daughter cell receives too many or too few chromosomes.

In **telophase** the chromosomes uncoil again. Around the two sets of chromosomes, new **nuclear envelopes** form, and the nucleoli also form anew. This completes the division of the nucleus, karyokinesis. After this comes **cytokinesis**, the division of the cytoplasm. In animal cells a **contractile ring** of actin and myosin under the membrane tightens and pinches the cell in two daughter cells.

gewusst: The name mitosis comes from the German scientist Walther Flemming, who observed the division of the nucleus closely in the 19th century.
In our body countless cells divide every day, for example in the skin and in the gut.
