teile.einleitung: The body needs micronutrients only in small amounts, but they are vital. They include vitamins and minerals. If they are missing, you can fall ill even if you eat enough.
wichtigste: Micronutrients include vitamins and minerals.
According to the WHO, iron deficiency is the most common deficiency in the world.
Iron is needed in haemoglobin for carrying oxygen.
The body needs vitamin K for blood clotting.
On a vegan diet you have to supplement vitamin B12.
A severe lack of vitamin B1 leads to beriberi.
Calcium is the most common mineral in the body.

abschnitte.text: Food gives us **macronutrients** such as carbohydrates, fats and proteins. They give energy. **Micronutrients**, on the other hand, are needed by the body only in tiny amounts. These include **vitamins** and **minerals**. Minerals of which we need only traces are called **trace elements**, for example iron, zinc or iodine. Micronutrients provide no energy but are needed for many processes in the body.

**Iron** is found in the red blood pigment **haemoglobin**. It is needed so that the blood can **carry oxygen**. According to the **WHO**, **iron deficiency** is the most common deficiency of a micronutrient in the world. It makes you tired and pale. **Calcium** is the mineral that occurs in the largest amount in the body. Most of it is in the **bones** and teeth. Dairy products are a good source.

The body needs **vitamin K** for **blood clotting**, so that wounds stop bleeding. It is found mainly in green vegetables. **Vitamin B12** occurs almost only in foods from animals. Anyone on a **vegan** diet therefore usually has to take it as a **supplement**. **Folic acid** is another B vitamin that is important for cell division and the making of blood.

A severe lack of **vitamin B1**, also called **thiamine**, leads to the disease **beriberi**. It damages nerves and the heart. In the past it often occurred where people ate mainly polished white rice. Another example is scurvy, from a lack of vitamin C. In Switzerland, **iodine** has been added to table salt for over a hundred years, to prevent iodine deficiency and goitre.

You can eat enough calories and still get too few micronutrients. This is called **hidden hunger**. It affects very many people around the world, especially where the diet is one-sided. It is best prevented with a **varied diet**: plenty of vegetables, fruit, wholegrain, pulses and, depending on the way you eat, dairy products, fish or meat.

gewusst: Sailors used to get scurvy on long voyages until people noticed that citrus fruits help against it.
In 1922 Switzerland was among the first countries to introduce iodised table salt.

teile.einleitung: Melatonin is a hormone that tells our body that it is night. It is made mainly in the dark and helps to steer the day and night rhythm. It is made chiefly in the pineal gland in the brain.
wichtigste: Melatonin is made mainly in the pineal gland.
The pineal gland looks like a small pine cone.
The melatonin level is highest in the middle of the night.
The body makes melatonin from serotonin.
In old age the production at night usually decreases.
For many animals, melatonin also shows the season.
Melatonin is also found in plants.

abschnitte.text: Melatonin is made mainly in the **pineal gland**. It is only about the size of a pea and lies deep in the brain. It gets its name from its shape: it looks like a small **pine cone**. In German, another word for the stone pine is “Zirbel”, and the gland is named after it. The pineal gland receives information through nerves about whether the eyes are seeing light at that moment or not.

Melatonin was discovered in the 1950s. Researchers found that a substance from the pineal gland **lightens the dark skin of frogs**. It draws together the pigment granules in the skin cells. That is why the hormone was given the name **melatonin**, after the Greek word for “black”. In humans it does not have this effect on skin colour, though.

The body makes melatonin from the messenger substance **serotonin**. When it gets dark, the production rises. The melatonin level is highest **in the middle of the night** and falls again towards morning. Bright light, including from screens, slows the production. In this way melatonin helps to steer the **sleep and wake rhythm**. In **old age**, less melatonin is usually made at night.

In winter the nights are longer, so melatonin is made for longer. In this way melatonin can show many animals the **season**. This helps them, for example, to prepare for hibernation or to change their coat. It is astonishing that melatonin is found **in plants too**. It is found, for example, in cherries, tomatoes and some nuts.

Melatonin does not stay long in the blood. It is broken down mainly in the **liver** and then passed out through the kidneys. That is why the level falls quickly in the morning, when no new melatonin is being made. Melatonin is also available as a medicine, for example against jet lag. In Switzerland it needs a prescription and should only be taken after medical advice.

gewusst: The French philosopher René Descartes thought the pineal gland was the seat of the soul.
Even light at night, for example on a trip to the toilet, can briefly slow the making of melatonin.

teile.einleitung: The adrenal glands are two small hormone glands that sit like little caps on top of the kidneys. They make vital hormones such as adrenaline and cortisol. Without them the body could not react to stress and could not control its salt balance.
wichtigste: Every person has two adrenal glands, one on each kidney.
They make hormones such as adrenaline and cortisol.
An adrenal gland consists of two parts: the cortex and the medulla.
The adrenal medulla makes the stress hormones adrenaline and noradrenaline.
The adrenal cortex makes cortisol, aldosterone and small amounts of sex hormones.
The cortex is controlled by the brain through the pituitary gland.
The adrenal glands are indispensable for life.

abschnitte.text: The adrenal glands lie in the back of the abdomen, directly on the upper end of the kidneys. The right one is rather triangular, the left rather crescent-shaped. Each weighs only about 5 to 10 grams, about as much as a few coins. Despite their name, in German “Nebenniere”, which literally means “next to the kidney”, they do not belong to the kidney, but are **hormone glands** in their own right.

An adrenal gland is built like a fruit with a skin and a core. On the outside lies the **adrenal cortex**, on the inside the **adrenal medulla**. Both parts have quite different jobs and make different hormones. The medulla is closely linked to the nervous system and is directly controlled by nerves.

When you are startled or afraid, the adrenal medulla releases **adrenaline** within seconds. The heart beats faster, breathing becomes deeper and the muscles get more sugar as energy. This reaction is called the fight-or-flight reaction. It already helped early humans to flee from wild animals.

The cortex makes **cortisol**, which helps with longer-lasting stress and slows inflammation. Cortisol is highest in the morning and helps with waking up. The hormone **aldosterone** makes sure that the kidneys hold back salt and water. This keeps blood pressure stable.

If the adrenal cortex makes too few hormones, this is called **Addison’s disease**. People affected are very tired and weak and have to take hormones as tablets. If the body makes too much cortisol, Cushing’s syndrome arises. Such diseases are rare and are treated by specialist doctors.

begriffe.erklaerung: A messenger substance that travels through the body in the blood and gives orders to organs.
A stress hormone that puts the body on alert within seconds.
A hormone of the adrenal cortex that helps with stress and dampens inflammation.
A small gland at the brain that controls many other hormone glands.

gewusst: Around 1900 adrenaline was obtained in pure form as one of the very first hormones.
Cortisone, a medicine against inflammation, is closely related to the body’s own cortisol.
The Swiss chemist Tadeus Reichstein received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1950 for his research on hormones of the adrenal cortex.

teile.einleitung: Measles is an infectious disease caused by a virus. It is one of the most contagious diseases of all. Many people think of it as a harmless childhood illness, but it can be dangerous.
wichtigste: Measles is caused by a virus.
It is very contagious and is passed on through the air.
At the start you often have a fever, a cough and red eyes.
After that a red skin rash appears.
Koplik spots on the lining of the cheek are an early sign.
Usually you get measles at most once in your life.
The Swiss vaccination schedule recommends two doses.

abschnitte.text: Measles is caused by the **measles virus**. It is **very contagious**. When we cough, sneeze or talk, tiny droplets get into the **air**. Anyone who breathes them in can catch it, even if they were only in the same room for a short time. Almost all unprotected people who come into contact with the virus fall ill.

At first you feel as with a bad cold: **fever**, **cough**, a runny nose and **red, inflamed eyes**. An early sign is the **Koplik spots**. These are small whitish spots on the inside of the cheeks. A few days later a **red rash** appears. It usually begins behind the ears and on the face and spreads over the whole body.

Measles weakens the **immune system** for a longer time. That is why other illnesses can follow, such as **pneumonia** or an ear infection. Rare but very dangerous is **inflammation of the brain**. It can leave lasting damage. Even today people around the world still die of measles, above all small children in poorer countries.

Anyone who has had measles once is usually protected for life afterwards. So you get it **at most once**. But it is much safer to be vaccinated. The **Swiss vaccination schedule** recommends **two doses**, usually combined with protection against mumps and rubella. If enough people are vaccinated, the virus can hardly spread any more. This also protects babies who are still too young for the vaccination.

gewusst: After a cough, the measles virus can stay infectious in the air of a room for up to two hours.
Because measles is so contagious, very many people have to be vaccinated so that the disease does not spread.

teile.einleitung: The thigh bone is the longest and strongest bone of the human body. It joins the hip to the knee. Doctors call it the femur.
wichtigste: The thigh bone is the strongest bone in the body.
Every person has two of them, one in each leg.
The technical term is femur.
It joins the hip and the knee.
It is about a quarter as long as the whole body.
The round upper end is called the head of the femur.

abschnitte.text: The **thigh bone** is **long and tube-shaped**. Experts call it the **femur**. It measures about **a quarter of body height**. In an adult of 1.80 metres it is therefore about 45 centimetres long. Every person has **two** of them, one in each leg.

At the top the bone carries the round **head of the femur**. It sits in a socket of the pelvis and forms the **hip joint**. Between the head and the shaft lies a sloping section, the **neck of the femur**. At the bottom the thigh bone meets the **shin bone** at the **knee**. At the front there lies the kneecap.

abschnitte.titel: Strong and able to bear loads
abschnitte.text: In walking, running and jumping the thigh bone carries the weight of the body. That is why it is especially **strong**. Powerful muscles attach to it, for example the large muscle at the front of the thigh that straightens the knee. Inside the bone is **bone marrow**, in which blood cells are made.

Because the bone is so strong, in young people it usually breaks only under great force, for example in road accidents. In older people, on the other hand, it is often the **neck of the femur** that breaks after a fall. Then an operation is usually done so that the person can soon walk again.

gewusst: The thigh bone can bear very large loads, many times body weight.
From the length of a thigh bone experts can roughly calculate how tall a person was.

teile.einleitung: Muscles can become stronger and thicker if you train them. In **muscle building**, training, nutrition and recovery work together. If one of them is missing, the muscle hardly grows.
wichtigste: Through strength training the muscle fibres become thicker, which is called hypertrophy.
Protein is the most important nutrient for muscle building.
The muscles grow mainly in the recovery phase.
Supercompensation means that the body recovers beyond its old level.
Unused muscles waste away, which is called atrophy.
During sleep the body repairs the muscles that have been put under strain.
Humans have about 650 skeletal muscles.

abschnitte.text: Depending on how you count, humans have over 600 **skeletal muscles**, and about **650** is often given. They are fixed to the bones by **tendons**. Tendons transfer the force of the muscle to the bone, while ligaments join bone to bone. Skeletal muscles can be controlled **at will**, and only they are built up in a targeted way with strength training. Heart and smooth muscles work by themselves.

If a muscle is strongly challenged, it adapts. The individual **muscle fibres** become thicker, which is called **hypertrophy**. As a result the muscle becomes bigger and stronger. The opposite is called **atrophy**, the wasting of muscle. Muscles that are not used for weeks, for example because of a plaster cast, become thinner and weaker. With training they can be built up again.

The training only gives the **stimulus**, and growth happens in the **recovery phase**. After a strain the body does not just recover, it even becomes a little more capable than before. This principle is called **supercompensation**. That is why breaks between training sessions are important. Especially valuable is **sleep**: then the body releases growth hormones and repairs the muscles that have been put under strain.

Muscles consist to a large part of **protein**. The body needs it to build new muscle substance after training. Good sources of protein are dairy products, eggs, meat, fish, pulses and nuts. In addition the body needs enough energy from carbohydrates and fat. Anyone who eats a varied diet usually gets enough protein.

gewusst: The largest muscle of the human body is the gluteus maximus.
Children and young people too can safely build up strength with exercises using their own body weight.

teile.einleitung: Even with our eyes closed we know how our arms and legs are lying. The **muscle spindles** help with this. These small sense organs in the muscle measure how long a muscle is at the moment and how quickly it is being stretched.
wichtigste: Muscle spindles measure the length and stretching of the muscle.
Inside them lie intrafusal fibres.
Gamma motor neurons set their sensitivity.
Ia fibres pass on the signals of the primary endings very quickly.
The patellar tendon reflex is based on muscle spindles.
The Golgi tendon organ, on the other hand, measures tension.

abschnitte.text: Muscle spindles are **stretch receptors**. They lie parallel to the normal working fibres in the muscle. If the muscle is stretched, the spindles are stretched too and report this to the spinal cord. In this way the nervous system learns how long a muscle is and how quickly its length is changing. This is important for the **sense of position** and for finely tuned movements.

abschnitte.titel: The structure of a muscle spindle
abschnitte.text: A muscle spindle is surrounded by a capsule. Inside lie special fibres, the **intrafusal fibres**. The normal working fibres outside are called **extrafusal**. According to how their cell nuclei are arranged, two types are told apart. In **nuclear bag fibres** the nuclei are gathered in the middle, and in **nuclear chain fibres** they lie one behind the other in a row. Sensory nerve endings wind around the fibres.

The primary, spirally wound endings are joined to thick, very fast conducting **Ia fibres**. They bring the reports to the spinal cord. The intrafusal fibres are steered by **gamma motor neurons**. These tighten their ends and so set the sensitivity of the spindle. In a voluntary movement **alpha and gamma motor neurons** are activated together. In this way the spindle stays tight even when the muscle shortens and keeps reporting.

If the doctor taps the tendon below the kneecap with a small hammer, the muscle at the front of the thigh is briefly stretched. The spindles report this through Ia fibres to the spinal cord. There the fibre ends directly at the **alpha motor neuron**, which makes the muscle twitch. The leg shoots forwards. Because there is only **one synapse** in between, this **patellar tendon reflex** is especially fast. The **Golgi tendon organ** at the transition from muscle to tendon, on the other hand, mainly measures the tension and reports it through Ib fibres.

gewusst: A reflex like the knee tendon reflex takes place without the brain first thinking about it.
Muscles for fine movements, for example in the hands and neck, contain especially many muscle spindles.

teile.einleitung: Melanocytes are the pigment cells of the skin. They make the pigment melanin and distribute it to the surrounding skin cells. In this way they determine our skin colour and protect against UV radiation.
wichtigste: Melanocytes lie mainly in the stratum basale of the epidermis.
Their precursors come from the neural crest.
Melanin is made in organelles called melanosomes.
The key enzyme is tyrosinase.
Through branched projections they pass the pigment on to keratinocytes.
One melanocyte supplies about 36 keratinocytes.
In vitiligo, melanocytes are lost in sharply bordered patches.

abschnitte.text: The **epidermis**, the outer layer of the skin, consists of several layers. The melanocytes lie mainly in the lowest layer, the **stratum basale**. There they sit between the ordinary skin cells, the **keratinocytes**. Their precursors come from the **neural crest**. This is a tissue from which parts of the nervous system also arise. From there the cells move into the skin even before birth.

Melanocytes make the pigment **melanin** in small sacs, the **melanosomes**. The starting material is the protein building block **tyrosine**. The most important enzyme in this is **tyrosinase**. If it is missing or does not work, no melanin is made. This is the case in one form of **albinism**. Sunlight stimulates the melanocytes to make more melanin.

Melanocytes have long, **branched projections**, like the branches of a tree. Through these projections they pass the melanosomes on to the surrounding **keratinocytes**. One melanocyte supplies about **36 keratinocytes** in this way. In the keratinocytes the melanosomes settle like a **cap** above the cell nucleus. In this way they protect the **DNA**, the genetic information, in particular from UV radiation.

abschnitte.titel: Why skin is different shades of dark
abschnitte.text: People with dark skin do **not have clearly more melanocytes** than people with light skin. What matters is the **amount and kind of melanosomes**. In dark skin they are bigger, more numerous and contain more dark melanin. They are also broken down more slowly in the keratinocytes. This gives a great variety of skin colours.

In **vitiligo**, also called the **white patch disease**, melanocytes are lost in certain areas. **Sharply bordered white patches** appear on the skin. The disease is not contagious and is usually not painful. It is thought that the body’s own immune system attacks the melanocytes. The affected places are especially sensitive to the sun.

gewusst: Melanocytes also sit in the hair roots, and they colour the hair.
The cap of melanin above the cell nucleus works like a little parasol for the genetic information.

teile.einleitung: A quick sprint, a sudden stop, and straight away something pulls in the thigh. Often this is a **muscle strain**. It is one of the most common sports injuries and usually heals well if it is treated properly.
wichtigste: A muscle strain is an overstretching of the muscle.
A torn muscle fibre is more serious than a strain.
Typical is a sudden, pulling, cramp-like pain.
After the injury stop the sport at once.
The first-aid rule PECH, as it is called in German, stands for rest, ice, compression and elevation.
Not warming up raises the risk.
A slight strain heals in a few days to a few weeks.

abschnitte.text: In a **muscle strain** the muscle is stretched beyond its normal length. Very fine injuries arise, but no visible tear. More serious is a **torn muscle fibre**, in which individual fibres really do tear. It takes longer to heal. Typical for a strain is a suddenly shooting, **pulling, cramp-like pain** that gets worse with movement.

Strains arise especially often in **fast sprints and changes of direction**. Sudden, explosive movements such as bursts of speed or stops put the muscle under heavy strain. The thighs and the calves are often affected, for example in football, floorball or tennis. A big risk is **not warming up**. Cold, unprepared muscles stretch less and are injured more easily. Tiredness also plays a part.

Anyone who feels a strain should **stop the sport at once**. That way the muscle is not damaged any more. Then the rule **PECH** helps. In German the letters stand for **P**ause (rest), **E**is (ice), **C**ompression with a pressure bandage and **H**ochlagern (elevation). You never put the ice directly on the skin, but wrapped in a cloth. Cooling and pressure help to keep the swelling small.

A slight strain usually heals in **a few days to a few weeks**. After that you should **put the muscle under load again slowly** and not train fully at once. With strong pain, a dent in the muscle or a large bruise you should see a doctor. You can prevent strains with good **warming up**, regular training and enough recovery.

gewusst: The PECH rule is also known in Swiss sports clubs and in the training of Youth and Sport.
In English a similar rule is called RICE, which is also the word for the grain.

teile.einleitung: Macrophages are cells of the immune system. They eat germs, dead cells and foreign bodies. This makes them something like the body’s refuse collection and its guard force at the same time.
wichtigste: Macrophages are made from monocytes, a kind of white blood cell.
The name means “big eater” in Greek.
They recognise bacteria using, among other things, Toll-like receptors.
They kill bacteria they have taken in with reactive oxygen species.
In the spleen they break down old red blood cells.
Alveolar macrophages clean dust from the alveoli.
In tuberculosis they form granulomas around the germs.

abschnitte.text: The word **macrophage** comes from Greek and means **“big eater”**. Macrophages develop from **monocytes**. These are white blood cells that swim in the blood. When they move out of the blood into the tissue, they become macrophages. There they take in foreign material and waste by wrapping themselves around it. This process is called **phagocytosis**.

abschnitte.titel: How they recognise and kill bacteria
abschnitte.text: Macrophages carry special feelers on their surface, the **Toll-like receptors**. With these they recognise typical parts of bacteria, for example the **lipopolysaccharide** from the shell of some bacteria. A bacterium that has been taken in ends up in a sac that fuses with a lysosome. This forms a **phagolysosome**. In it the bacterium is killed and digested using, among other things, **reactive oxygen species**.

Macrophages are found in almost all organs, and they often have names of their own. In the alveoli live the **alveolar macrophages**. They clear away dust particles and germs that have been breathed in. In the **spleen**, macrophages mainly break down old **red blood cells**. In doing so, the iron from the blood pigment is recovered and used again.

Experts roughly distinguish two kinds. **M1 macrophages** promote inflammation and kill bacteria especially effectively. **M2 macrophages** help rather to end inflammation and repair tissue. Macrophages also show other defence cells fragments of the germs. In this way they help to start the targeted defence of the immune system.

Sometimes macrophages also contribute to diseases. In the walls of the blood vessels they can soak up fat. They are then called **foam cells**. They contribute to **arteriosclerosis**, a narrowing of the arteries. In **tuberculosis**, macrophages cannot completely kill the germs. Instead, together with other cells, they wall them off in a little nodule, the **granuloma**.

gewusst: Macrophages in the body break down huge amounts of old red blood cells every day.
The scientist Ilya Mechnikov described the eating cells and received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for it in 1908.

teile.einleitung: Lysosomes are tiny sacs in animal cells. They act like the cell’s digestion and recycling station. With acid enzymes they break down old cell parts and substances that have been taken in.
wichtigste: Lysosomes contain acid hydrolases, enzymes that break down many substances.
Inside, the pH value is about 4.5 to 5.
Proton pumps in the membrane keep the acid conditions going.
In autophagy, the cell breaks down its own damaged parts.
When a phagosome fuses with a lysosome, a phagolysosome forms.
Christian de Duve discovered lysosomes in the 1950s.

abschnitte.text: A **lysosome** is a small sac surrounded by a membrane. Inside it there is an **acid pH value** of about **4.5 to 5**, clearly more acid than in the rest of the inside of the cell. **Proton pumps** in the membrane see to this. They constantly pump hydrogen ions into the lysosome. Lysosomes contain numerous enzymes, the **acid hydrolases**. They can break down proteins, fats, sugars and genetic material.

Lysosomes break down substances that the cell has taken in from outside. When an eating cell eats a bacterium, for example, it first lies in a sac, the **phagosome**. When this fuses with a lysosome, a **phagolysosome** forms, in which the bacterium is digested. In **autophagy** the cell breaks down its **own damaged parts**. It can use the building blocks again.

Lysosomal enzymes are dangerous, because they could digest the cell itself. But if they get into the **cytoplasm**, they usually do only little damage. The reason: there the pH value is **neutral**, and at a neutral pH these enzymes are **hardly active**. This is how the cell protects itself from its own tools.

The Belgian scientist **Christian de Duve** discovered lysosomes in the **1950s**. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1974 together with others. If a single lysosomal enzyme is missing or **faulty**, undigested substances build up in the cell. This gives rise to **lysosomal storage diseases** such as **Tay-Sachs disease**. They are rare and usually inherited.

gewusst: The name “lysosome” comes from Greek and means roughly “dissolving body”.
A Nobel Prize was awarded in 2016 for research on autophagy.

teile.einleitung: **Graves’ disease**, in German called Morbus Basedow, is a disease of the thyroid gland. The body’s own immune system constantly drives the thyroid on, so that it makes too many hormones. This is called an overactive thyroid.
wichtigste: Graves’ disease is an autoimmune disease of the thyroid gland.
Autoantibodies stimulate the TSH receptor and cause an overactive thyroid.
The Merseburg triad consists of a goitre, bulging eyes and a racing heart.
In English the disease is named after Robert Graves, and in German after Carl von Basedow.
The TSH value is strongly lowered in an overactive thyroid.
It is treated with thiamazole, radioiodine therapy or an operation.

abschnitte.text: The **thyroid gland** lies at the front of the neck and makes hormones that steer the metabolism. Normally the pituitary gland gives the signal for this with the hormone **TSH**. In Graves’ disease the immune system makes **autoantibodies** that stimulate the TSH receptor. They imitate TSH and constantly drive the thyroid on. The many thyroid hormones inhibit the pituitary gland, so the **TSH value is strongly lowered**. The antibodies still drive the gland on.

In an overactive thyroid the **metabolism runs at full speed**. People affected often lose weight although they have a good appetite. Restlessness, sweating, trembling and a fast pulse are added. The doctor **Carl von Basedow** from Merseburg described three typical signs in 1840: an enlarged thyroid (**goitre**), bulging eyes (**exophthalmos**) and a racing heart. They are called the **Merseburg triad**. Not all sick people show all three signs.

In some people affected, the eyes are also involved. This **endocrine orbitopathy** arises because tissue and muscles behind the eye swell and push it forwards. The eyes can then be red, dry or sensitive to light. **Smoking** makes the involvement of the eyes clearly worse.

Medicines such as **thiamazole** belong to the antithyroid drugs. They inhibit the building of iodine into the thyroid hormones, so the production of hormones falls. In **radioiodine therapy**, the thyroid takes up radioactive iodine-131 and is irradiated from the inside. This ends the overactivity for good. Another possibility is an **operation** in which the thyroid is removed wholly or in part.

gewusst: The Irish doctor Robert Graves described the disease as early as 1835, which is why it is called Graves’ disease in English.
The thyroid gland needs iodine to make its hormones.

teile.einleitung: **Crohn’s disease** is a chronic, that is, long-lasting, inflammation in the digestive tract. It comes in flare-ups and can affect any section from the mouth to the anus. Together with ulcerative colitis it belongs to the chronic inflammatory bowel diseases.
wichtigste: Crohn’s disease can affect the whole digestive tract from the mouth to the anus.
Most often affected is the terminal ileum, the end of the small intestine.
Healthy and inflamed sections alternate.
The inflammation reaches through all layers of the intestinal wall.
Typical complications are fistulas.
Smoking clearly raises the risk and the severity.
The disease is named after Burrill B. Crohn.

abschnitte.text: In **Crohn’s disease** the digestive tract is inflamed again and again. The disease usually runs in **flare-ups**, between which there are calmer times. Typical complaints are stomach pain, diarrhoea, tiredness and loss of weight. Crohn’s disease is not contagious. The exact causes are not yet fully understood, and a combination of genes, the immune system, gut bacteria and the environment is suspected.

Crohn’s disease can affect **any section** of the digestive tract, from the mouth to the anus. Most often it is the **terminal ileum** that is affected, the transition from the small intestine to the large intestine. That is why the disease used to be called ileitis terminalis too. Typical is **discontinuous** involvement: inflamed sections alternate with healthy ones, which is called skip lesions. **Ulcerative colitis**, on the other hand, is confined to the large intestine and spreads continuously.

The inflammation is **transmural**, which means it affects all layers of the intestinal wall. As a result it can bore through the wall and form passages to other organs or to the skin. Such passages are called **fistulas**, and they often occur around the anus. Collections of pus and narrowings of the intestine can also arise. Under the microscope one often finds **granulomas without caseation**, small nodules of defence cells.

**Smoking** raises the risk and leads to more severe courses, so stopping smoking is part of the treatment. In 2001 the gene **NOD2** was described as the first genetic risk factor. NOD2 helps the defence system to recognise parts of bacteria. The disease is named after the American doctor **Burrill B. Crohn**, who described it in 1932 with colleagues. So far Crohn’s disease cannot be cured, but medicines can calm the inflammation well.

gewusst: Crohn’s disease often begins as early as in the teenage years or as a young adult.
In Switzerland, a large research study has for years followed people with chronic inflammatory bowel diseases.

teile.einleitung: On almost every food packet there is a date. The **best-before date** says until when a product safely keeps its quality. But it is not an expiry date after which you have to throw everything away.
wichtigste: The best-before date is the date until which a product keeps its quality.
On the packet it usually says “best before”.
Until this date the manufacturer guarantees the quality.
The date applies only to the unopened packet that has been stored correctly.
Foods that spoil easily carry “use by” instead.
After the best-before date you check a product by looking, smelling and tasting.
Table salt normally carries no best-before date.

abschnitte.text: The **best-before date** is a promise from the manufacturer. Until this day the food keeps its qualities such as taste, smell, colour and nutritional value. On the packet it usually says “best before” with the date. Important: the date applies only to the **unopened packet** that is stored correctly, for example cool or dry. After opening, a product can spoil more quickly.

For foods that spoil easily, such as minced meat, fresh poultry or raw fish, there is a different statement: **“use by”**. This is the use-by date. After this day you should no longer eat the product, even if it still looks good. This is because **dangerous germs** may have formed that you can neither see nor smell. These two statements are also used in Switzerland.

When the best-before date has passed, a food is often still edible. You check it with your senses: **look, smell and taste**. A yoghurt that looks normal, smells normal and tastes normal can usually still be eaten. If the lid is bulging, it smells strange or mould shows, it belongs in the bin. Anyone who goes about it like this throws away less food unnecessarily.

abschnitte.titel: What keeps for a long time
abschnitte.text: Dry foods such as **pasta**, rice or sugar often keep long beyond the date if stored dry. Fresh meat, fish and raw milk, on the other hand, spoil quickly. Some foods need no best-before date at all, for example **table salt**, because it practically does not spoil. Fresh fruit and vegetables also usually carry none.

gewusst: A large part of the food that is thrown away would still be edible, and products often end up in the bin because of a passed best-before date.
Sugar and salt hardly ever spoil, because germs find hardly any water in them to live on.

teile.einleitung: Lymph is a pale liquid that flows through the body in vessels of its own. It collects surplus tissue fluid and brings it back into the blood. On the way it is filtered in the lymph nodes.
wichtigste: Lymph is a pale liquid in the lymph vessels.
It is made from tissue fluid.
At the end it flows into the venous blood near the heart.
Lymph nodes filter the lymph and fight off germs.
Lymph contains particularly many lymphocytes.
In the intestine, lymph takes up fats in particular.

abschnitte.text: A little liquid constantly leaks out of the finest blood vessels into the tissue. It supplies the cells. Most of it returns to the blood, but a remainder stays in the tissue. This **tissue fluid** is taken up by fine **lymph vessels** and is then called **lymph**. It is pale, usually almost transparent. Without lymph vessels the tissue would swell.

The lymph vessels join up into ever larger channels. The largest lymph channel in the body is called the **thoracic duct**. At the end the lymph flows **into the venous blood near the heart**. Lymph has no heart of its own to pump it. It is driven along mainly by the **movements of the muscles around it**. Little valves make sure that it does not flow backwards.

On its way the lymph flows through many **lymph nodes**. These **filter** the lymph and **fight off germs**. Lymph contains particularly many **lymphocytes**, a kind of white blood cell. In a **sore throat** the lymph nodes in the neck often swell, because they are fighting the germs there.

In the intestine, lymph has a special job. It takes up **fats** from food in particular. After a meal rich in fat, the lymph from the intestine therefore looks milky white. This is how the thoracic duct got its German name, the “milk-chest duct”. Through it the fats finally reach the blood.

gewusst: Several litres of lymph flow through the body every day.
Movement helps lymph to flow, which is why legs swell more easily when you sit still for a long time.

teile.einleitung: Nail scissors are small scissors for shortening fingernails and toenails. They are part of personal care, because nails that are too long break off easily or collect dirt.
wichtigste: Many nail scissors have slightly curved blades.
Instead of scissors you can also use nail clippers.
Rough edges are smoothed with a nail file.
You cut fingernails slightly round and toenails rather straight.
You cut fingernails about every one to two weeks.
Every person should have their own nail scissors.
Nail scissors are kept safely in a case.

abschnitte.text: Nail scissors are small and handy. Many have **slightly curved blades**. This lets you cut fingernails nicely round, to fit the shape of the fingertip. The blades are **pointed and sharp**. That is why small children should only use nail scissors with the help of a grown-up.

Instead of scissors many people use **nail clippers**. They press two sharp edges together and cut the nail off. After cutting, the edges can be rough. With a **nail file** you rub them smooth. That way you do not catch on jumpers or socks. For babies there are scissors with rounded tips.

You cut **fingernails** **slightly round**, following the shape of the finger. **Toenails**, on the other hand, you cut rather **straight**. If the corners of toenails are cut too round, they can grow into the skin. You do not cut too short, and a narrow white edge may stay. After a bath the nails are softer and easier to cut.

Nails grow slowly but steadily. That is why you cut fingernails about **every one to two weeks**. **Germs or fungi** can cling to nail scissors. It is best, therefore, for every person in the family to have their **own scissors**. You clean them now and then and keep them in a **case**. That way the pointed scissors are protected, and nobody pricks themselves on them.

gewusst: Fingernails grow faster than toenails, about twice as fast.
Nail scissors are often made of stainless steel.

teile.einleitung: In kidney failure the kidneys no longer work properly. They filter the blood too little, and waste substances stay in the body. The disease can appear suddenly or develop slowly over years.
wichtigste: A distinction is made between acute kidney failure and chronic kidney disease.
The most common causes of the chronic form are diabetes and high blood pressure.
The severity is measured by the filtering performance eGFR, and below 15 ml/min it is called kidney failure.
When substances that should be passed in urine build up in the blood, it is called uraemia.
In the final stage only dialysis or a kidney transplant helps.

abschnitte.text: In **acute kidney failure** kidney performance falls within hours or days. A **prerenal** cause lies “before the kidney”, for example a heavy loss of fluid, so that too little blood arrives. The acute form can often recover. **Chronic kidney disease** develops slowly and usually cannot be reversed. The most common causes are **diabetes** and **high blood pressure**.

Doctors estimate the filtering performance with the **eGFR**, the estimated glomerular filtration rate. It is given in millilitres per minute. Depending on the value the disease is divided into stages G1 to G5. Below 15 ml/min there is **stage G5**, kidney failure. An early warning sign is **albumin** in the urine: then the kidney filter lets protein through that it otherwise holds back.

If the kidneys are weak, waste substances collect in the blood. This is called **uraemia**. Typical too is **hyperkalaemia**, a potassium level that is too high, which can disturb the heart. The balance of calcium and phosphate is thrown into disorder, and the bones are weakened. This bone disease is called **renal osteopathy**. Often anaemia also arises, because the kidney makes less of a hormone that stimulates the making of blood.

Early on it is important to control blood pressure and blood sugar well. In the final stage the work of the kidneys has to be replaced. In **dialysis** a machine or the peritoneum cleans the blood, usually several times a week. The better solution is often a **kidney transplant**, that is, a donated kidney.

gewusst: A person can live well with only one healthy kidney.
Chronic kidney disease causes no complaints for a long time and is often discovered by chance in a blood test.

teile.einleitung: A night light is a small lamp that glows faintly at night. It helps you find your way in the dark and gives many children a safe feeling.
wichtigste: A night light gives a little light in the dark.
Faint, warm light disturbs sleep least.
Many night lights are plugged straight into the socket.
Night lights without a cable need a battery or a rechargeable battery.
A light sensor switches some night lights on in the dark.
The moon is a natural night light.
The body sleeps best in a dark room.

abschnitte.titel: What a night light is for
abschnitte.text: A night light glows only **faintly**. It is not so bright that you could read, but you can make out furniture, doors and the way to the toilet. That way you do not stumble in the night. Many children are **afraid** in a completely dark room. A small light calms them and helps them to fall asleep.

Many night lights are plugged directly into the **socket**. Others have no cable and need a **battery** or a **rechargeable battery** in which the electricity is stored. Some night lights have a **light sensor**. It notices when it gets dark and switches the lamp on by itself. In the morning it goes off again. Today most night lights glow with economical **LEDs**.

**Darkness** tells the body that it is night. Then it makes the sleep hormone **melatonin**. Bright and bluish light, on the other hand, keeps you awake. That is why a **faint, warm** light in yellow or orange is best for the night. It is best not to put the night light right next to your head. You sleep deepest when the room is as dark as possible.

The **moon** is a natural night light. It does not glow by itself, but is lit by the **sun** and throws this light back. At full moon it is so bright outside that you can see paths and trees well. Fireflies, too, make a small light in warm summer nights.

gewusst: Fireflies are really beetles that make their light themselves.
Moonlight is nothing other than sunlight thrown back.
